However, hunting and eating of birds has been observed on occasion.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Zora|first1=Anna|last2=Gerlach|first2=Justin|date=2021-08-23|title=Giant tortoises hunt and consume birds|journal=Current Biology|language=English|volume=31|issue=16|pages=R989–R990|doi=10.1016/j.cub.2021.06.088|issn=0960-9822|pmid=34428417|doi-access=free|bibcode=2021CBio...31.R989Z }}</ref> Pet tortoises typically require diets based on wild grasses, weeds, leafy greens and certain flowers. Certain species consume [[worm]]s or [[insect]]s and carrion in their normal habitats. Too much protein is detrimental in herbivorous species, and has been associated with shell deformities and other medical problems. Different tortoise species vary greatly in their nutritional requirements. Behavior Communication in tortoises is different from many other reptiles. Because they are restricted by their shell and short limbs, [[visual communication]] is not a strong form of communication in tortoises. Tortoises use [[Olfaction|olfactory cues]] to determine the sex of other tortoises so that they can find a potential mate. [[Haptic communication|Tactile communication]] is important in tortoises during combat and courtship. In the book, Krishna reported that he had had a Kuṇḍalinī awakening in 1937–38.{{sfn|Borkataky-Varma|Foxen|2025|pp=164, 206}}<ref name="Krishna 1971">{{cite book |last=Krishna |first=Gopi |author-link=Gopi Krishna (yogi) |title=Kundalini: The Evolutionary Energy in Man |place=Boulder, Colorado |publisher=[[Shambhala Books]] |year=1971 |orig-year=1967}}</ref> His metaphysics echoed what Vivekananda, Yogananda, and Aurobindo had set out, but his book was unique, according to Borkataky-Varma and Foxen, in "the detail and immediacy of his experiential narration."{{sfn|Borkataky-Varma|Foxen|2025|p=165}} In his introduction to the book, the scholar of religion [[Frederic Spiegelberg]] "famous[ly]"{{sfn|Borkataky-Varma|Foxen|2025|pp=168–169}} described Krishna as "an extremely honest reporter, to the point of humbleness" who describes "the bewildering landscape around him, colorfully, truthfully, without really knowing exactly what he has found."{{sfn|Borkataky-Varma|Foxen|2025|pp=168–169}} Gopi

changes.text: …and not our own."<ref name="Woodroffe 1950"/> === [added: Carl Jung, psychoanalysis, and psychiatry === [[File:ETH-BIB-Jung, Carl Gustav (1875-1961)-Portrait-Portr 14163 (cropped).tif|thumb|left|upright=0.8|The [[Psychoanalysis|psychoanalyst]] [[Carl Jung]] held an influential 1932 seminar on Kundalini Yoga.<ref name="Jung Shamdasani 1999"/>]] Western awareness of Kuṇḍalinī was strengthened by the interest of the Swiss [[Psychoanalysis|psychoanalyst]] [[Carl Jung]] (1875–1961), who held a 1932 seminar on Kundalini Yoga for the Psychological Club in [[Zurich]].<ref name="Jung Shamdasani 1999">{{cite book |last=Jung |first=Carl Gustav |author-link=Carl Jung |editor-last=Shamdasani |editor-first=Sonu |editor-link=Sonu Shamdasani |title=The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga: Notes of the Seminar Given in 1932 by C.G. Jung |date=1996 |location=Princeton, New Jersey |publisher=[[Princeton University Press]] |isbn=978-0-691-02127-0 |pages=xviii-xix, xxvi}}</ref> In the introduction to her edited version of Jung's seminar, [[Sonu Shamdasani]] wrote that [[depth psychology]] developed at the same time as Western awareness of yoga texts, as psychoanalysts sought to break free from the confines of Western thought.<ref name="Jung Shamdasani 1999"/> Reviewing the book, Davi Nichol commented that the seminar {{Blockquote|text="was widely regarded as a milestone in the psychological understanding of Eastern thought and of the symbolic transformations of inner experience. Kundalini yoga presented Jung with a model for the developmental phases of higher consciousness, and he interpreted its symbols in terms of the process of [[Individuation#Carl_Jung|individuation]], with sensitivity towards a new generation's interest in alternative religions and psychological exploration."<ref name="Nichol 1996">{{cite journal |last=Nichol |first=Davi |title=Book Review: ''The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga: Notes of the Seminar Given in 1932 by C.G. Jung'' (Princeton University Press, 1996) |journal=Psychoanalytic Books: A Quarterly Journal of Reviews |issue=10 |date=1999}}</ref>}} According to Jung, "the concept of Kundalini has for us only one use, that is, to describe our own experiences with the unconscious."<ref name="Hayman">{{cite book |last=Hayman |first=Ronald |title=A Life of Jung |date=2001 |publisher=[[W. W. Norton & Company|W. W. Norton]] |location=New York |isbn=978-0-393-32322-1 |page=[https://archive.org/details/lifeofjung00haym/page/304 304] |url=https://archive.org/details/lifeofjung00haym |url-access=registration |quote=the concept of Kundalini has for us only one use ...}}</ref> Jung used the Kundalini system symbolically as a means of understanding the dynamic movement between conscious and unconscious processes.<ref name="Jung Shamdasani 1999"/> According to Shamdasani, Jung claimed that the symbolism of Kuṇḍalinī yoga suggested that the bizarre symptomatology that patients at times presented, actually resulted from the awakening of the Kuṇḍalinī. He argued that knowledge of such symbolism enabled much that would otherwise be seen as the meaningless by-products of a disease process to be understood as meaningful symbolic processes, and explicated the often peculiar physical localizations of symptoms.<ref name="Jung Shamdasani 1999"/> The popularization of eastern spiritual practices has been associated with psychological problems in the west. [[Psychiatry|Psychiatric]] literature states that "since the influx of eastern spiritual practices and the rising popularity of meditation starting in the 1960s, many people have experienced a variety of psychological difficulties, either while engaged in intensive spiritual practice or spontaneously."<ref name="Turner 1995">{{cite journal |last1=Turner |first1=R. P. |last2=Lukoff |first2=D. |last3=Barnhouse |first3=R. T. |last4=Lu |first4=F. G. |title=Religious or spiritual problem. A culturally sensitive diagnostic category in the DSM-IV |journal=[[The Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease]] |date=July 1995 |volume=183 |issue=7 |pages=435–444 |doi=10.1097/00005053-199507000-00003 |pmid=7623015}}</ref> Among the psychological difficulties associated with intensive spiritual practice we find "Kundalini awakening," "a complex physio-psychospiritual transformative process described in the yogic tradition."<ref name="Turner 1995"/> Researchers in [[transpersonal psychology]]<ref name="Scotton 1999"/> have described a complex pattern of sensory, motor, mental, and affective symptoms associated with the concept of Kundalini, sometimes called the Kundalini syndrome.<ref name="Greyson 1993">{{cite journal |last=Greyson |first=Bruce |title=Near-death experiences and the physio-kundalini syndrome |journal=[[Journal of Religion & Health]] |date=1993 |volume=32 |issue=4 |pages=277–290 |doi=10.1007/BF00990954 |pmid=24271550}}</ref> Spiritual emergency associated with Kuṇḍalinī awakening may be viewed as an acute [[psychotic episode]] by psychiatrists who are not conversant with the culture. The biological changes of increased [[P300 (neuroscience)|P300]] amplitudes that occur with certain yogic practices may lead to acute psychosis. Biological alterations by Yogic techniques may be used to warn people against such reactions.<ref name="Bharadwaj 2012">{{cite journal |last=Bharadwaj |first=Balaji |title=Proof-of-concept studies in Yoga and mental health |journal=International Journal of Yoga |date=2012 |volume=5 |issue=1 |page=74 |doi=10.4103/0973-6131.91719 |doi-broken-date=8 November 2026 |pmc=3276938 |pmid=22346071 |doi-access=free }}</ref> ===] Aurobindo === [[Sri Aurobindo]] (1872…

kind.added_text: Carl Jung, psychoanalysis, and psychiatry === [[File:ETH-BIB-Jung, Carl Gustav (1875-1961)-Portrait-Portr 14163 (cropped).tif|thumb|left|upright=0.8|The [[Psychoanalysis|psychoanalyst]] [[Carl Jung]] held an influential 1932 seminar on Kundalini Yoga.<ref name="Jung Shamdasani 1999"/>]] Western awareness of Kuṇḍalinī was strengthened by the interest of the Swiss [[Psychoanalysis|psychoanalyst]] [[Carl Jung]] (1875–1961), who held a 1932 seminar on Kundalini Yoga for the Psychological Club in [[Zurich]].<ref name="Jung Shamdasani 1999">{{cite book |last=Jung |first=Carl Gustav |author-link=Carl Jung |editor-last=Shamdasani |editor-first=Sonu |editor-link=Sonu Shamdasani |title=The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga: Notes of the Seminar Given in 1932 by C.G. Jung |date=1996 |location=Princeton, New Jersey |publisher=[[Princeton University Press]] |isbn=978-0-691-02127-0 |pages=xviii-xix, xxvi}}</ref> In the introduction to her edited version of Jung's seminar, [[Sonu Shamdasani]] wrote that [[depth psychology]] developed at the same time as Western awareness of yoga texts, as psychoanalysts sought to break free from the confines of Western thought.<ref name="Jung Shamdasani 1999"/> Reviewing the book, Davi Nichol commented that the seminar {{Blockquote|text="was widely regarded as a milestone in the psychological understanding of Eastern thought and of the symbolic transformations of inner experience. Kundalini yoga presented Jung with a model for the developmental phases of higher consciousness, and he interpreted its symbols in terms of the process of [[Individuation#Carl_Jung|individuation]], with sensitivity towards a new generation's interest in alternative religions and psychological exploration."<ref name="Nichol 1996">{{cite journal |last=Nichol |first=Davi |title=Book Review: ''The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga: Notes of the Seminar Given in 1932 by C.G. Jung'' (Princeton University Press, 1996) |journal=Psychoanalytic Books: A Quarterly Journal of Reviews |issue=10 |date=1999}}</ref>}} According to Jung, "the concept of Kundalini has for us only one use, that is, to describe our own experiences with the unconscious."<ref name="Hayman">{{cite book |last=Hayman |first=Ronald |title=A Life of Jung |date=2001 |publisher=[[W. W. Norton & Company|W. W. Norton]] |location=New York |isbn=978-0-393-32322-1 |page=[https://archive.org/details/lifeofjung00haym/page/304 304] |url=https://archive.org/details/lifeofjung00haym |url-access=registration |quote=the concept of Kundalini has for us only one use ...}}</ref> Jung used the Kundalini system symbolically as a means of understanding the dynamic movement between conscious and unconscious processes.<ref name="Jung Shamdasani 1999"/> According to Shamdasani, Jung claimed that the symbolism of Kuṇḍalinī yoga suggested that the bizarre symptomatology that patients at times presented, actually resulted from the awakening of the Kuṇḍalinī. He argued that knowledge of such symbolism enabled much that would otherwise be seen as the meaningless by-products of a disease process to be understood as meaningful symbolic processes, and explicated the often peculiar physical localizations of symptoms.<ref name="Jung Shamdasani 1999"/> The popularization of eastern spiritual practices has been associated with psychological problems in the west. == Common name ==

Bidalasana/Bitilasana, also called Marjariasana/Bitilasana, ... is far better known as Cat/Cow pose in yoga as exercise. If Google hits can be trusted, that "far better" is perhaps a million times better, but it depends to an extent which terms one searches on. Still, there seems little doubt that the English name would be a no-brainer of a better choice here, so I'll move the article now and create a selection of the more likely redirects. [[User:Chiswick Chap|Chiswick Chap]] ([[User talk:Chiswick Chap|talk]]) 12:39, 3 May 2026 (UTC)

== Lead image of a school should be of the school ==

An editor is attempting to replace the lead image of the school with a heraldic device. The article is about a school, per its title, not heraldry, so the lead image should be of the school. [[User:Chiswick Chap|Chiswick Chap]] ([[User talk:Chiswick Chap|talk]]) 22:36, 3 May 2026 (UTC)

::::Given the documented range of spellings, no lexicographer is going to say that one of them is "correct", as usage plainly varies both between and within countries: as [[User:Plantdrew|Plantdrew]] notes, "chili" is more commonly used in the cited sources. The claim to an "original" spelling and meaning does not help as it falls to the [[etymological fallacy]] (that because something was once spelt in a certain way and had a certain meaning, it must continue like that), but spellings and meanings both evolve. In one specific case, the dish [[chili con carne]] is usually written as shown, but it too varies. All we can do is to acknowledge those facts. === Comments ===

* <s>The article, although short, embodies quite a serious problem of structure as all 3 of the main sections (i.e. barring the 'History') contain discussions of the same issue, namely slippage and failure with certain types of line or rope:
::: 'Properties': no good for HMPE/dyneema/nylon monofilament; remedy = more turns (triple knot?)
::: 'Uses': no good for HMPE/aramid; remedy = triple knot
::: 'Security': no good for ([[Kernmantle rope]]s) Spectra/Technora cores; remedy = triple knot
: Clearly these need to be discussed in one section, i.e. the body of the article needs to be restructured from the existing 3-section (post-History) arrangement.</s>
:::: I've rearranged the article to only have two sections after the history section. The 'security' section was moved to 'properties' and I took a sentence about slippage out of the 'uses' section.

* <s>In 'Properties', the issue of untying/jamming when tightened is mentioned in both paragraphs before sliding (if that's the word) into related matters. This needs rewriting to make each point once in an orderly way.</s>
::If that is intended as a pun, its very subtle, I appreciate it. I've reworked the section quite a bit with the merge of material from the other two sections.

* <s>The aside {{tq|(cordelette)}} needs to be explained with its climbing context and properly integrated in the text; an illustration would make sense here to show what the term means and how the knot functions in this situation.</s>
:: I've added a picture and more of an explanation of what cordalettes are used for with a wikilink.

* <s>The use of three similar and somewhat repetitive infoboxes is undesirable; the information so presented would be better in a comparative table to avoid repetition, not to mention the lengthy use of screen real-estate down the side of a large part of the text. Really there should be at most 1 infobox, specially as it's agreed they are all closely related (or the merge would have been a mistake).</s>

== Medical-sounding claims not from a [[Systematic review]]; [[WP:OR|Original research]] ==

An editor has now repeatedly attempted to get some material on the medical-sounding topic "Connective tissue physiology" into the article as a top-level chapter, supported initially by [[WP:PRIMARY]] sources which are plainly not sufficient to meet [[WP:MEDRS]]. The material was then reworked with medical language and reinserted cited to an article in ''[[Physical Therapy journal|Physical therapy]]''. I would not like to say whether that journal is appropriate for any sort of medical-sounding claim. 

In addition, half of the material was uncited, reading like [[WP:OR|Original Research]], the editor's personal interpretation. The source cited is paywalled, but a search does not support the presence of "Yin Yoga" in that source: if indeed it is not mentioned there (and there is no hint of it in the abstract) then this is pure editorial, which is forbidden on Wikipedia. To be clear, policy specifically forbids the making of any inference, however simple it may appear, from what a source says (about a piece of research, say) to what it might possibly mean in the world (such as when yoga is practised). 

A further serious issue is that claims are being made for the effectiveness of a practice without [[Systematic review]] which is not just any kind of review: it is a systematic analysis of the quality of the evidence (such as it may be) presented by researchers in the field, with conclusions about whether the claims can be sustained strongly, weakly, or not at all. Such a systematic review rejects evidence that is from informal trials or experiments that lack a proper [[Treatment and control groups|control group in their experimental design]]; and it is likely that it would challenge any evidence that is not secured with a [[Blinded experiment|double-blind controlled trial]], something that is difficult to achieve with a physical practice. 

For these reasons (either of which would be sufficient), I've deleted the material from the article. 

An additional point is that it is quite unacceptable for an editor to make repeated attempts to insert challenged material into an article. Once they are aware, because of a deletion and an edit comment, that material is challenged, the only options are discussion on the talk page or to drop the attempt: anything else is [[WP:DISRUPTIVE|disruptive editing]]. == Variability alone is of no interest ==

An editor has now repeatedly added a claim about variability of leg length, with no explanation of why this may have arisen or what function it serves. Every species has a mass of alleles and phenotypic variability, which we cannot possibly document, nor should we: that's a task for genomic and other databases. == [[PNAS]] paper by Margulis et al is mainstream science ==

An editor has seen fit to try to remove a brief mention of a research article in [[PNAS]] in 2006, asserting it's "fringe". However, PNAS is a (highly) respected mainstream journal with a robust scientific peer-review process. Now it may well be that the paper's proposal is incorrect: science goes like that. The appropriate response for mainstream science mistakes, if such it be, is not editorial censorship ("we know best"), but the addition of later sources that question or refute the proposal made. Since "once notable, always notable" is a correct Wiki-slogan, we do not go about deleting relevant accounts of an idea's history; instead, we update them from the latest sources. :All the parthenogenetic offspring's alleles come from the mother. An allele is a form of a specific gene. Say there are 2 alleles of two genes (A and B). The mother is heterozygous for one gene, Aa (with two alleles), and homozygous for the other, BB (with one allele). The offspring could be AABB or aaBB, both of which mean it has less allele diversity than its mother. You can see that if the mother was heterozygous for a lot of genes, the offspring are likely to have close to half her alleles; if she was homozygous for all of them, the offspring must have all her alleles. === Comments === * The text contains a lot of TLAs (three-letter acronyms), ranging from some like [[RNA]] that may be familiar to many readers (still worth spelling it out, ribonucleic acid), to quite a few that will certainly be new to nearly all visitors to the page (DAg, RNP, and the more complex S-DAg, L-DAg, not to mention HDAg, HBsAg which are a struggle even for this biologist). It would be better to spell these out and to introduce them gently. * Here's an example: {{tq|Ribozyvirians have negative-sense single-stranded RNA (–ssRNA) genomes that are about 1.5–1.7 kilobases in length. The genome is a non-segmented, covalently-closed circular RNA (cccRNA) molecule that organizes into a rod-like shape due to a high amount of self-complementarity.}} The [https://hemingwayapp.com/readability-checker Hemingway readability checker] says the first sentence is "hard to read" and the second "very hard to read". It rates the sample Grade 15 ("Poor. Aim for 9.") and states that the average adult's reading level is 8 or 9. To reword this material, consider some of the terms that readers will not know: '''negative-sense'''; '''single-stranded RNA'''; genome (perhaps); '''kilobase'''; '''covalently-closed'''; '''cccRNA'''; '''self-complementarity'''. The same goes for much of the rest of the text. * The article would be much easier for Joe Public* to read with a new 'Context' section (just after the lead). The context should explain that life is cellular, but that viruses, while behaving like parasites, are not cells and are doubtfully even living. You can explain briefly that a virus is a bit of DNA or RNA packaged in an envelope; and that the envelope contains proteins which enable the virus to stick on to a cell and allow its DNA or RNA to enter the cell and start to replicate itself. I think you also need to have a small paragraph in 'Context' explaining what a [[ribozyme]] is, that they are capable of catalysing chemical reactions, including splicing bits of RNA itself. You can see that there is a lot here that readers need to know to read the rest of the article, so try to make it simple, clear, and richly wikilinked. And reliably-sourced. ::::: * Joe Public can read the ''Baseball Gazette'' and has heard of viruses which give you 'flu
and get into your computer. He may have heard of DNA somewhere. :* I've tried to make sure acronyms are introduced in an appropriate manner and tried to make the text less technical either through explanation or using wikilinks, including adding a sentence explaining what ribozymes are. I'm not sure an entire section for context is needed. It would be excessive for every virus article to have something like that and people generally know that viruses are different from cells, they've heard of DNA and RNA, and so on. And this is a more technical article, so a lot of technical terms are bound to be used. ::* This is missing the key point that technical articles in a global encyclopedia *must* be accessible to a "broad audience": this article is not. See 'Summary' below for Wikipedia policy on this. ::* This review is of this one article. Arguments about what might be needed in other articles are out of scope, but there is no reason whatever why context should not be supplied in any technical article; minimal context for understandability is by definition not "excessive". * You've said ''Kolmioviridae'' is the sole family in ''Ribozyviria'' twice. ** Reworded. * {{tq|a variety of animals, including amphibians, birds, fish, insects, mammals, and reptiles.}} Why not say "[[insect]]s and a wide range of [[vertebrate]]s, including ...", for clarity. ** Done. * Both the virion diagram and the 'Structure' section's text are rather unclear about the helper and its proteins. Why not say up front that the [[hepatitis B virus]] (please wikilink in text and in caption) is the helper, and that it supplies multiple (apparently *all*, from the diagram) envelope proteins. * It seems there are [[spike protein]]s protruding (a little) from the envelope, and the spikes aren't much like the familiar and visibly spiky spikes of COVID-19. (Actually, looking at the other sources, the proteins aren't round at all, the diagram is very diagrammatic... we should have a better diagram really.) It isn't clear, either, which of the three HBsAg envelope proteins is the spike protein: all three seem to be dotted about individually rather than arranged in spikes. The current text and the diagram caption need rewording in harmony to make these things clear. ** I added a sentence for this and the prior point and tried to clarify the spike protein vs envelope protein language. * The virion diagram would be much better if the label "Hepatitis Delta Virus proteins" were added next to the wrapping of little HDAg circles around the RNA, and if "Hepatitis B proteins" were added just outside the envelope with HBsAg circles of varying sizes and colours. At the moment the diagram-text relationship is needlessly obscure, when (given what is written later) it's actually quite simple. Actually I might tweak the diagram and you can review the result. **The diagram has one flaw: you put "Hepatitis Delta Virus's own protein's (Ribozymes)". The ribozymes are genomic and antigenomic. They're not proteins separate from the RNA. The blue dots are nucleocapsid proteins (S-DAg, L-DAg), not ribozymes. *** Tweaked. * {{tq|pleomorphic in shape}} - 99% of readers won't know what that is. Please gloss. ** Done. *** You've added text in the following sentence, but the reader coming to the pleomorphic sentence for the first time will still be in the dark. === Small comments === * Format "kolmio" as {{lang|fi|kolmio}} to identify and display it correctly. ** Done. * Spell out "Greek letter Δ" as "Greek letter Δ (Delta)" for readers who don't read Greek. ** Done. * Wikilink [[International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses]]. ** Done. * Wikilink [[Eugene Koonin]]. ** Done. === Images === * Ribbon diagram - PD * Hepatitis D virions - CC-by-4.0. == Bringing some order to Kundalini-related articles ==

I've taken a tour around Wikipedia's Kundalini-related articles (including [[Prana]], [[Pranayama]], [[Chakra]], and so forth), and have found it quite disordered. Major texts were barely mentioned; citations were haphazard and often incomplete; illustrations were patchy; explanations were sketchy, missing, or contradictory; Wiki-voice was used for the opinion of one modern yoga school, or one particular medieval text, but not for others; dates were largely absent; and the articles neither flowed logically, nor matched what was at the other end of many of the provided wikilinks. 

Accordingly, I'm working to improve the clarity and reliability of our coverage of these topics. I've added timelines, diagrams, and photographs; documented gurus with their dates; filled in many citations; reduced overlaps; added explanations and sources; and paraphrased several very lengthy quotations. This remains a work-in-progress, but I hope editors will find the articles somewhat more approachable already. Any assistance in improving the articles further will be warmly welcomed. 

One specific issue is that this article, [[Kundalini Yoga]] (an evidently ambiguous title), overlaps markedly with the [[Kundalini]] article. It could be argued that any yoga practice which acknowledges Kundalini (certainly from the time of the ''Hatha Yoga Pradipika'', and possibly earlier) could be called 'Kundalini Yoga', while more recently, multiple yoga gurus have taught something called 'Kundalini Yoga' but incorporating their own selection of beliefs and practices. This means that it is not clear what we should have in an article entitled "[[Kundalini Yoga]]" that is not in the Kundalini article. 

It would be possible to create several subsidiary articles on subtopics such as [[Kundalini Yoga (Yogi Bhajan)]], [[Kundalini Yoga (Guru Jagat)]], [[Kundalini Yoga (Sri Aurobindo)]], and so on, but it is not clear that this would be practical or (given the mainly primary sourcing for each such variant), actually encyclopedic. I suggest therefore that for the moment we simply merge [[Kundalini Yoga]] into [[Kundalini]]: or rather, make it a redirect, as the two articles already substantially overlapped, and after the work I've done to clarify, fill out, and organise the Kundalini article, it basically covers both the pre-modern and the modern history and concepts, so it spans the various meanings of 'Kundalini Yoga' in the wider context of an explanation of Kundalini itself. 

To get things into a consistent state, I'll make this a redirect now, and will have a think about which articles it would be desirable to create to make the topic area clearer. One such is ''[[The Serpent Power (book)]]'', on the 1919 book by 'Arthur Avalon'. No doubt you will have further ideas for new articles. [[User:Chiswick Chap|Chiswick Chap]] ([[User talk:Chiswick Chap|talk]]) 15:47, 5 November 2026 (UTC)

== Samādhi section needs to focus on Patanjali's Ashtanga ==

This article is about Patanjali's Ashtanga, of which his version of Samādhi is the 8th limb. Samādhi can (plainly) be taken much more widely to include e.g. the extensive Buddhist coverage of that topic: but that is not part of Patanjali's 8-fold system, [[Ashtanga (eight limbs of yoga)]]. In other words, we have in the [[Ashtanga (eight limbs of yoga)#Samādhi]] chapter an extensive coatrack which is actually off-topic for this particular article; it would no doubt be splendid as part of a separate, non-Patanjali article on the wider subject. We need to cut it down and hive off the non-Patanjali coverage here; and to ensure it is properly cited. Joshua, you may well be correct about scope, but as your question implies, different interpretations are possible, and we do not seem to be converging on a solution that way, not least because the section is already long and difficult. Could I therefore propose that we take a step back and consider how best to proceed.

==== 3 possible approaches ====
Firstly, I hope we can agree that the coverage of '8. Samādhi' is already considerably longer than that of the Ashtanga limbs 1. to 7.: it is around 880 words long, whereas for example '7. Dhyāna' is 250 words, '3. Āsana' is 240 words, and '6. Dhāraṇā' is only 90 words. 

Given the agreed [[WP:UNDUE]] tag on the section, this all means that the section '8. Samādhi' is around three times the desired length. 

The section is not only long but complex, technical, and hard to read. For instance the sentence {{tq|Vitarka (or avitarka) "deliberative," "with thought": According to the later commentarial tradition, citta is concentrated upon a gross object of meditation, an object with a manifest appearance that is perceptible to our senses.}} is 33 words. The [https://hemingwayapp.com/readability-checker Hemingway readability checker] scores it as "Post-graduate. Poor... very hard to read", with the advice "Aim for [school grade] 9". This means that it is unsuitable for Wikipedia's general readership.

There are three possible approaches to resolve this situation.

: A. Cut down the text to a simple summary of 250 words. 

: B. Move the text to a new subsidiary article '[[Samadhi in the Yoga Sutras]]'; write a simple 250-word summary of its text in its lead section; replace the current text of '8. Samādhi' with the wording of that lead section, supported by citations from the text.

: C. Merge the text to the existing article of wider scope, '[[Samadhi]]'. Draft a simple 250-word summary of the part of it which applies specifically to Patanjali's view of the topic, and replace the existing text of '8. Samādhi' with that summary.

I've marked the link to the '[[Samadhi]]' article as "broader" not just "further"; the '[[Samadhi in the Yoga Sutras]]' would be the "further" link. I hope this is all clear, and that we can agree on one of the three approaches. [[User:Chiswick Chap|Chiswick Chap]] ([[User talk:Chiswick Chap|talk]]) 09:04, 13 November 2026 (UTC)

=== Comments ===

I see you have created this article, expanding on the migration section in the [[Christmas Island red crab]] article. The topic is notable and there seems to be enough reliable coverage of the migration to make a separate article worthwhile. The text is clear and readable, and seems to be suitably cited. I have only a few comments to make for this to become a GA.

* <s>The infobox gives four pairs of co-ordinates; this implies that there are 4 locations for the migration, which needs to be stated (and cited) in the article's text. You should make clear with suitable sources whether there are specific beaches and land corridors that the crabs follow every year, for example, and say what these are.</s>
: Removed.

* The lead begins {{tq|The Christmas Island crab migration is a red crab migration...}}: but the label "red crab" links to [[Christmas Island red crab]] (''Gecarcoidea natalis''). This is somewhat less clear than it should be. I suggest a) that we write "The [[Christmas Island red crab]] migration is a migration of the land crab, ''[[Gecarcoidea natalis]]''... "; b) that (after this GAN has completed) we rename the article to "[[Christmas Island red crab migration]]". (The GAN will automatically close with fail if you rename it now.)
: 

* The lead provides cited context about the crabs' migration that is not repeated in the article body. Please move all the citations to a 'Context' section in the body, with a version of the text which might be somewhat expanded to set the migration comfortably in context for the general reader. 

* The 'Threats' section coverage of crazy ants needs to be mentioned briefly in the lead. 
: 

* <s>The article gives much space to bridges, tunnels, and protection, implying that '''human activity is a major threat''' to the crabs survival on migration. A paragraph on that threat needs to be added to the 'Threats' section.</s>
: Done.

* You might want to wikilink "formic acid", "biological control" and "parasitic wasp" among other technical terms used in the article.
: 

* <s>{{tq|a five-metre and five centimetres bridge}} is a curious phrase, and it isn't clear what it means: width? length? 5m length and 5cm width? I see from the sources that it's actually a metal bridge 5m high and of unspecified width and length, so the 5cm seems like an error (or an earlier joke). A photo in the first source shows a steep (near-vertical) approach on either side of the bridge, with mesh for the crabs to climb up. Some clarification is needed.</s>
: Fixed.

* <s>Earwig's copyvio checker reports "violation unlikely".</s>

* <s>The portals box is running into the References. I suggest simply removing it as unnecessary (you have provided an excellent selection of wikilinks for navigation already), and the box is interfering with the display of the references. Failing that you could put it into External links; as we have no ordinary external links (to websites etc), it would be best to format the links there like "<nowiki>{{portal-inline|Australia}}</nowiki>" (and so on for any others), and do the same for the Commons link (ie use commons-inline).</s>
: Done.

* <s>Plenty more has been written about the migration. You might want to consult {{cite magazine |last=Hicks |first=John W. |title=Red Crabs: On the March on Christmas Island |magazine=[[National Geographic (magazine)|National Geographic]] |pages=822–831 |volume=172 |issue=6 |date=December 1987 |oclc=643483454 |ref=none<!--remove this parameter if citing-->}} for a popular account. You might further like to look at some of the scholarly research on the migration, such as listed at [https://scholar.google.co.uk/scholar?hl=en&as_sdt=0%2C5&q=Gecarcoidea+natalis+migration&btnG= Google Scholar]. I'd suggest you at least add a 'Migration biology' section to the article to summarize some of the key research findings.</s>

:* The new section needs a bit more work to make it an account of the actual biology; by naming it 'Studies' you reflect what you have written, but what the article needs is instead a 'Biology' section which explains 
::: a) how migration comes about with its hormonal control, timing, etc, and you integrate your Princeton study on rainfall;
::: b) how the crabs navigate back to the right place(s), and you integrate your bit on tracking and straight lines;
::: c) how the crabs have the strength to migrate (do they feed up for months beforehand?) and you integrate your bit on energy from JEB.
::: d) you move your BBC earth bit to 'Threats', if it actually adds anything there (not much, I think)
: 

* The list of external links is becoming rather long, and we should probably not have more than one link per agency (i.e. at most one from ABC, one from BBC, one from Google, etc).

== The Yoga family of articles ==

Hi, I noticed your edit to [[Yoga]]. That article is unsurprisingly at the head of a large family of articles, covering branches of classical, hatha, and modern yogas and a wide range of related topics, including many asanas and social issues. These last cover topics such as commercialisation, politics, and cultural appropriation. There is thus a hierarchy [[Yoga]] - [[Modern yoga]] - [[Yoga as exercise]] - [[Yoga in society]] - ... all the society topics ... so appropriation is no fewer than 4 levels down the tree (for instance, there are some 200 Yoga as exercise articles, not counting [[Asana]]s). You'll appreciate that each of these many articles has to be written neutrally, explaining the various points of view ([[WP:NPOV]]) making use of reliable sources ([[WP:RS]]) on its particular topic. Appropriation is a sensitive topic and widely differing opinions have been expressed on it; there isn't room up at the top of the tree to do it justice, nor to cover the various sources appropriately. I've therefore undone your edit to Yoga, but thought it would be helpful to let you know the context, and that the topic has in fact been covered in detail already. All the best, [[User:Chiswick Chap|Chiswick Chap]] ([[User talk:Chiswick Chap|talk]]) 07:41, 30 April 2026 (UTC)

== [[Conifer]] and related groups ==

Hi, you are making taxonomic edits to these articles, either wholly uncited or with citations in odd places. The procedure is 1) to update the main text of the article, and cite it; 2) to update cladograms, diagrams, and images, based on the same citations (and repeating the refs as needed); and 3) to update the lead and infobox ... in that order. It's no good doing "lead engineering" or "taxobox engineering" when this doesn't reflect the cited text, that just creates inconsistency and more problems down the line. 

The other thing is, these changes are clearly somewhat controversial: there has been doubt about the gnetophytes' taxonomic rank for over a century. Rather than just eliding all the history and claiming that authority Z said T so T must be "true", it'd be far better to state clearly that there has been doubt, that X said t1, Y said T2, and Z said T3. That gives a much fairer picture, not pretending that things are clearer than they are. All the best, [[User:Chiswick Chap|Chiswick Chap]] ([[User talk:Chiswick Chap|talk]]) 07:48, 23 May 2026 (UTC)

== Tolkien, sources, and a tree of articles ==

Hi, I noticed the kerfuffle that followed your addition of some material on Finnish influences on Tolkien to the top-level [[J. R. R. Tolkien]] article. Your edit comment "added information without a source" was certainly true, which poses the question "Why?". 

Firstly, you must be aware that Wikipedia requires claims to be cited to [[WP:RS|reliable sources]]. You must surely also have noticed that the Tolkien article is highly conspicuous, and has indeed been formally reviewed, so every claim there, other than yours, was already suitably sourced. So, you can't really be surprised that an editor has already removed your unsourced material: anyone is free to do that at any time, without notice.

Secondly, if you follow a few of the many wikilinks in the Tolkien article, you will quickly discover that there are '''hundreds''' of articles in WikiProject Middle-earth, with that article at the top. Thus, there is a whole article called [[Influences on Tolkien]], which in turn links to articles on Beowulf's influence, and influences from Finnish, the classical world, Celtic, Shakespeare, and so on and so forth :

* [[J. R. R. Tolkien]]
** [[Influences on Tolkien]]
*** [[Beowulf and Middle-earth]]
*** ...
** [[Themes of The Lord of the Rings|Themes of ''The Lord of the Rings'']]
*** [[Sound and language in Middle-earth]]
*** ...

This means that the tree of articles contains '''much''' more material than could possibly be included at the top level. Your uncited addition was too detailed for the top level, or to put it another way inappropriately positioned in there, as well as uncited. It is in fact already covered in full, with a quotation and a source, in the appropriate place in the tree. 

Hope this is all clear to you. All the best, [[User:Chiswick Chap|Chiswick Chap]] ([[User talk:Chiswick Chap|talk]]) 07:03, 8 July 2026 (UTC)

:Thanks for discussing; there is no need to feel disappointed, as I'll explain. The topics are both notionally "correctness of language", but I note that they are rather dissimilar: the first is an in-universe constructed language, and the second concerns registers of English. 
:On the use of Quenya in Wikipedia, I think we have to be careful to stay within the real world rather than going in-universe. I recognise that there are thousands of lovers of artificial language, and thousands more Tolkien fans, who would like to include every minute detail of Quenya grammar. But for Joe M. Public (Wikipedia reader), even the word "Noldor" is at the limit of comprehensibility, and if understood at all, Joe will very likely read it as synonymous with "Elves" or indeed with "some group or other of Tolkien characters". The word "Noldo", especially if used exactly once, will be taken as either a typographic error for "Noldor", or an obscure bit of language of uncertain meaning, inserted by an overenthusiastic Tolkien fan. In short, we should not wish to go there on Wikipedia. I've adjusted the grammar to avoid any perceived need for "Noldo" (even if we were following Quenya grammar).
:On the use of the formal register of English, we need to consider whether formality is actually required in Wikipedia articles. English Wikipedia is unique in that it is widely consulted by people whose native language is not English. Compare Finnish or Swedish Wikis, for example, and you will appreciate that we editors of the English Wiki have to write not just for a public that wants a quick, simple overview of a topic, but who need it in very plain English. For me, that means that formal, stiff, old-fashioned, and wordy written-only registers of English are inappropriate. Policy tells us to avoid contractions like "can't" and "it's", so we spell those out; but equally, we avoid "heretofore", "moreover", "therewith", and I'm afraid "whom" as unnecessarily difficult. "Correctness" is, you will find, remarkably hard to define, as there are many "correct" forms of English. Dictionaries such as the OED take care to explain that they do not dictate correctness, but instead describe native-speaker usage. For me, the correct register for Wikipedia is simple, plain, uncontracted, and avoids needless grammatical complexity. There you have it. All the best, [[User:Chiswick Chap|Chiswick Chap]] ([[User talk:Chiswick Chap#top|talk]]) 07:26, 8 July 2026 (UTC)

: Hi Chilicave, I'll see what I can do. 

The first thing I'd say at a casual glance is that if you'd told me it was a GA and you were working it up to FA, I'd not have been surprised; it looks to be in a reasonable state. So, getting it to GA shouldn't be too hard, I hope. 

If you're not familiar with the 6 GA criteria, you should make their acquaintance. The key questions are does it cover the main points of its subject, and is it reliably sourced throughout. The "main points" question requires some knowledge of the subject to answer; my guess is "yes" but the "Types" section does look a bit thin. The sources look suitable at a first glance. 

Some more detailed comments: 

=== Sources ===

The 'Sources' list covers some but not all of the books cited, which looks untidy. It would be best to move all the books there and to link to them (all) using the mechanism <nowiki>{{sfn|Boyce|1975|pp=147–191}}</nowiki> and so on. 

=== References ===

The references are uneven in multiple ways. To give a few examples among many:
* [8] Nigal, p. 81. lacks date (and should use the sfn template as above)
* [9] Drower, 1944:78 uses a non-standard format for page.
* [16] Hume again lacks date; there are many other examples.
* You sometimes have "pages", sometimes "P.", sometimes "p./pp.", and sometimes the pages are missing altogether (e.g. [44] Sinha 2008). 
* [39] bizarrely says "ISBN" but does not provide one. ISBN is actually optional, but if you're providing them for books then all the books should have them (or an OCLC if there is no ISBN for early books). 
* [43] Prinja 2009 does not correctly provide either the article title ("Weddings") nor the publisher ("BBC").
* Authors are sometimes given as Bloggs, Joe M.; sometimes as Joe M. Bloggs; and sometimes as Bloggs JM. I suggest we always use |last=Bloggs |first=Joe M. in the <nowiki>{{cite book |last= ...}}</nowiki> or equivalent template. 

=== Text ===

Suggest you move all the citations out of the lead; I notice that [1], [3], and [4] occur only in the lead, which is an error: everything in the lead should already be discussed and cited in the article body. That means that the lead should say nothing "new": if it's cited, that claim and citation are in the wrong place; if it's uncited, it's in the wrong place and is possibly [[WP:OR]] as well.

Once you've done that and tidied up the article body, revisit the lead and ensure it provides a coherent summary of the article's main points.

Agni is sometimes in italics, sometimes in roman.

All the texts named should be in italics.

In 'Upanishads', I suggest we have a transliteration into Latin characters (or IAST) beside the Devanagari text, with the translation beneath it. The existing "translation" is actually heavily interpreted, an "unpacking" translation at best, as immediately evidenced by its inordinate length: if we were to use such a thing, the interpretation would need to be reliably sourced, so I suspect it's unusable as it stands. Google Translate offers a transliteration and a direct translation:

<poem>ath yadyagnya ityachakshate bramacharyamev 
tadbramacharyen hyev yo dnyata tam 
vindate̕th yadishtamityachakshate bramacharyamev 
tadbramacharyen hyeveshtvatmanamanuvindate</poem>

<poem>Then if they call it sacrifice, it is celibacy 
That is the one who is known by celibacy
Then he finds what he desires, and they call it celibacy 
That, by celibacy, he worships and attains to himself</poem>

"Tadeusz Skorupski states" - who's he? We try to gloss and wikilink attributed authorities.

Why do "yagam" and "yagnam" redirect here? They're not found anywhere in the article, so either they should be added (and cited) in the text, or the hatnotes and the redirects should be deleted. 

Having the incomprehensibly [[Delphic ambiguity|Delphic]] hatnote "For concurrent Hindu usage, see [[Homa (ritual)]]" is not satisfactory, as there is plainly some relationship between the two things, and that relationship needs to be explained in a paragraph of cited text (maybe even a whole section called '== Ritual context ==' or something of that kind). Something important seems to be missing there.

'Types' first paragraph introduces several terms, but never explains any of them except śrauta  (which it links only later, and spells it differently). If the types are worth introducing then they must be clearly explained and differentiated (what are they and how/when are they each used?). The second paragraph partially explains "srauta" with an interpolation of yet another type not mentioned in the first paragraph, "Grhya" in the middle before the text returns to srauta again. The whole section needs to be rewritten for the average Wikipedia reader (Joe M. Public): Joe has heard of Hinduism and supposes it is quite like Buddhism, but never heard of yajna let alone of its subtypes. (I suspect Joe would have quite a lot of trouble with most of the other sections.)

'Method' mentions obliquely that the altar is "set in a mandapa or mandala or kundam," and the next sentence mentions that this encompasses a "square principle". The *very* determined reader can discover by searching for [[mandala]] that such things are square ... a link and an explanation are needed.

=== See also ===

Remove "yasna" as it's already discussed and linked in the text. Also "vedi"; maybe others.

=== Images ===

Diagrams must be big enough to be readable; the sacrificial space diagram was too small so I've adjusted it, but it needs redrawing with larger text labels (should be made in PowerPoint and saved to an SVG file, then uploaded to Commons), as even enlarged the text is very tiny.

The other images mostly seem relevant and well-chosen; they are on Commons and are plausibly licensed. The exception is "A miniature illustration of a falcon bird Athirathram yajna altar built using the square principle" which is uncited and not explained in the text. (Oh, "falcon bird" and "square principle" are mentioned higher up in the text, see 'Text' above, but it's really scrappy, and the bird's name is not mentioned or cited at all.) If it's relevant it needs to be explained a good deal more (why a falcon? who's Athirathram? what's the square principle? etc) and cited in a paragraph of text; if not, delete it.

The pair of images in 'Types' is headed "Different types of yajna" but it does not say what types they are, so it's unhelpful. The left image says its "Vedic" but it seems that applies to all yajnas? The other one has no hint of its type at all (and the image quality is, ahem, dreadful).

=== Summary ===

As always, the devil is in the detail. The article makes a worthy attempt at the subject, but in detail it is not coherent, not easy to follow, and does not seem to cover the topic; whether it covers the "main points" is not easy to ascertain. I suspect that quite a lot of rewriting will be necessary. Good luck! [[User:Chiswick Chap|Chiswick Chap]] ([[User talk:Chiswick Chap#top|talk]]) 09:28, 11 July 2026 (UTC)

== Making medical claims on Wikipedia ==

Hi, thanks for your intention to improve Wikipedia. 

However, people consult Wikipedia for reliable information, including on medicine, so people's safety is implicated. Accordingly, anything we claim must be exceptionally robustly based to ensure that articles never give the impression that a medication is safe and effective when those things have not been rigorously demonstrated to medical standards.

The rule is defined in the policy [[WP:MEDRS]]. Briefly summarized, it says you must not make any sort of medical claim without robust evidence from a [[Systematic review]]; in particular, you cannot just cite [[WP:PRIMARY]] research sources as these may be optimistic or unfounded. 

I've accordingly cut down or undone some of your recent edits. Hope this is clear. All the best, [[User:Chiswick Chap|Chiswick Chap]] ([[User talk:Chiswick Chap|talk]]) 12:58, 13 July 2026 (UTC)

kind.post_text: : Hi, thank you for your intention to improve Wikipedia's article [[Christopher Nolan's interpretation of The Odyssey|Christopher Nolan's interpretation of ''The Odyssey'']]. However, the material was uncited. Wikipedia relies entirely on the quality of its sources, as described in policy [[WP:V|on verifiability]]; this is achieved by [[WP:CITE|citing]] relevant sources, which are chosen [[WP:RS|to be reliable]]. Wikipedia requires editors to limit what they write to summaries of those sources; editorial opinion beyond that is considered to be [[WP:OR|original research]] beyond the scope of the encyclopedia. I hope this is clear; the upshot is that we need to cite any claim added to an article. == Still nowhere near Wikipedia quality ==

Hi, thanks for the intention to improve the article, but what you just added (the second time) is still nowhere near the required quality. Here is the material, cut from the article. Could I ask please that you work on it here (as you sort of implied above), and get it reviewed carefully (not just by me) before trying to add it again, as the repeated addition of raw un-Wiki-like material is fast becoming [[WP:DISRUPTIVE]]. Basically it would be best to attempt something much smaller (a single claim, a single citation, rather than a massive chunk of multiple sections). The reason for that is that there are many problems with: 

1) its structure, which should be with section and subsection headings using <nowiki>=== Section heading ===</nowiki> or <nowiki>==== Subsection heading ====</nowiki> as used here in this thread (but the article doesn't currently use subsections, so using them is basically deprecated).

2) its tone, which seems to be an editorial voice ("which appears to be a pure Nolan invention that is used 16 times in the movie." – which looks like pure "[[WP:OR|Original Research]]", forbidden on Wikipedia), not (as is required) a report of the views of scholars and critics (reliable secondary sources), nor even of Nolan (the primary source, to be used only in very small amounts, with caution and with direct attribution to page. This is a major and very serious problem with the current text, enough to have it immediately deleted even if all the other issues were fixed. 

3) its attempts at citations, which ought to be formatted using a template such as <nowiki>[[Template:Cite book]]</nowiki> complete with exact page number; other refs like <nowiki><ref>Various</ref></nowiki> are wholly unacceptable

4) formatting: we don't use boldface anywhere in articles except for the introductory phrase which reflects the article's name

5) the continued large amounts of uncited text.

6) the formatting of definitions as if this were a dictionary ([[WP:NOTDICT]]), or as if they were citations (they aren't)

7) the assembling of examples from primary sources to build up an argument, conveying an editorial opinion, is not allowed (Original Research by [[WP:SYNTH|Synthesis]]). This means that if you believe, say, that poem A and bible text B and literary text C all implicitly support conclusion D, that might be fine in a paper to a film society but is forbidden on Wikipedia. What you must do instead is to state that scholar S said that poem A is based on bible text B, and in S's stated view (which you might even quote) that means that conclusion D: but that requires you to find a suitable scholar S who actually wrote exactly that: you are not allowed to assemble the argument yourself, even if you believe the logic to be unassailable. Wikipedia, as an encyclopedia, is not a research platform, a news source, or a forum for arguing points of view. 

8) ... and so on. 

In other words, [[WP:CIR|a measure of Wiki-competence is required]], and the skill involved has many small components, all of which are unfortunately necessary to achieve an acceptable Wikitext. That can't be done in one giant leap, so it is necessary to learn in small steps. Hope this is clear, and sorry to bring what may seem like bad news. [[User:Chiswick Chap|Chiswick Chap]] ([[User talk:Chiswick Chap|talk]]) 18:16, 30 August 2026 (UTC)

I'd just note that claims must be cited to reliable sources; and concomitantly, that when an existing claim is cited to a reliable source, as at [[Poetry in The Lord of the Rings]], it is not satisfactory to update the claim from personal knowledge (or other uncited sources), as then the text will conflict with the existing source. == Improper move discussion at [[Talk:Alarm signal (animal communication)]] ==

Dear Helpful Cat, thank you for helping out at the proposed move of [[Alarm signal]]. I am sorry I didn't notice the discussion earlier but it was not posted where I'd have seen it (and I can't watch every Biology article). Here is what I've posted on the talk page: 

: 1) "This should have been more widely posted, such as to the relevant WikiProjects. 

: 2) The move should not have been conducted without checking the impact on articles linking to the moved article.

: 3) The hatnote at what is now "Alarm signal" correctly notes that a large number of articles link there: all the articles are using the term in the zoological sense, i.e. there was no practical ambiguity. 

: 4) The new disambiguation page "[[Alarm signal]]" actually lists only one article with "Alarm signal" in its name, so the move was incorrect and there was nothing to disambiguate. The two other entries are "[[Alarm device]]", an object that is never called "Alarm signal", and "[[Wake-up call]]" which could theoretically be called an alarm signal but which in practice is not called that. The two articles could simply be hatnoted to observe "For the animal communication, see 'Alarm signal'", but even those hatnotes are not necessary as the two terms "Alarm device" and "Wake-up call" are not ambiguous.

: In short, this move was a mistake, and it has created a) a pointless and incorrect disambiguation page (the terms are not ambiguous), and b) a large number of zoology articles with orange links to the incorrect disambiguation page, all of which would uniformly need fixing to become "Alarm signal (animal communication)". 

: I suggest we undo the mistaken move forthwith. This will leave the articles named above with correct unambiguous names, and will restore the mass of zoology articles that link to "Alarm signal" to a consistent and correct state."

The closing notice states "Editors desiring to contest the closing decision should consider a move review after discussing it on the closer's talk page." I am therefore here, and I suggest either a move review, or better that you undo the move and the close, as the arguments made do not hold water. [[User:Chiswick Chap|Chiswick Chap]] ([[User talk:Chiswick Chap|talk]]) 08:04, 23 September 2026 (UTC)

== Welcome! ==

Hello and [[Help:Introduction|welcome]] to Wikipedia!  I hope you like the place and decide to stay. Unfortunately, one or more of the articles you created, such as [[:Inundative application]], may not meet Wikipedia's [[Wikipedia:Core content policies|content policies]]. In short, to be included on Wikipedia, the topic of an article must be [[Wikipedia:Notability|notable]] and have been covered by published [[Wikipedia:Reliable sources|reliable]] and [[Wikipedia:Independent sources|independent sources]]. Articles must be written in a [[WP:NPOV|neutral manner]] and may not contain [[WP:NOLLM|AI generated material]].

Please read '''[[Help:Your first article|Your first article]]''' for an overview of the [[Wikipedia:Articles for creation|article creation process]]. The '''[[Wikipedia:Article wizard|Article Wizard]]''' is available to help you create an article for review. Note that articles are reviewed by volunteers and that it can take some time. If you'd like someone else to create an article, see [[Wikipedia:Requested articles|Requested articles]]. If you are stuck, come to the '''[[Wikipedia:Teahouse|Teahouse]]''', where experienced Wikipedians can help you through the processes.

New to Wikipedia? Please consider taking a look at [[Help:Introduction|our introductory tutorial]] or the page on [[Wikipedia:Contributing to Wikipedia|contributing to Wikipedia]]. Below are a few other good pages about article creation.
* [[Wikipedia:Article development|Article development]]
* [[Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Layout|Standard layout]]
* [[Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Lead section|Lead section]]
* [[Wikipedia:The perfect article|The perfect article]]
* [[Wikipedia:Task Center|Task Center]]{{snd}} for contributing to other articles. Writing a new article is tough, so getting experience elsewhere is useful.

I hope you enjoy editing here and being a [[Wikipedia:Wikipedians|Wikipedian]]! Please [[Wikipedia:Signatures|sign your name]] on talk pages using four tildes (<nowiki>~~~~</nowiki>); this will automatically produce your name and the date. If you have any questions, ask me on my talk page. You can also type '''{{tl|help me}}''' on this page, followed by your question, and someone will show up shortly to answer your questions. == Adding 'new' materials and citations to lead of [[Haplodiploidy]] ==

Hi, please don't add 'new' materials or citations to the lead of any properly-constructed Wikipedia article.

I see you're in your first 1,000 edits, so I hope you won't mind if I just run over the principles, apologies if you know most of it already.

* The lead is a summary, normally without repeating the citations, of the article body, which should be fully cited.

* As such, the lead should not contain anything 'new', whether text or citations.

* Citations are repeated from the body to the lead only in special situations, such as highly inflammatory topics (as with articles on countries that are at war, that sort of thing). Those citations are however already in the article body, and any statements in the lead are still summaries of usually more detailed text below.

* In very small, sketchy articles (sometimes very old, from the dawn of Wikipedia), there may be no section headings, so the article consists only of a brief body-text with no lead. That text must of course be cited (remedially, if it's an old uncited article). Best, if editing such a thing, is immediately to create section headings and add a brief summary as a new lead section.

Hope this is all clear and obvious, sorry for repeating anything you know.

I've therefore moved your new text and refs down into the article body. I think you'll see if you look down there that most of your points were in fact already covered, non-controversially, down there. I've moved all your refs, and one or two statements that seemed 'new' to the article. I hope you'll be pleased with the result. I don't see anything that immediately leaps out as needing additional summarising in the lead, but we can certainly discuss whether that would be necessary. All the best, [[User:Chiswick Chap|Chiswick Chap]] ([[User talk:Chiswick Chap|talk]]) 19:37, 10 October 2026 (UTC)

: Thanks for discussing. A botanical illustration has encyclopedic value for several reasons. A good botanical drawing brings together all the key aspects of a plant needed for study and identification, something that is hard to achieve in a photograph – photos are good for showing individual features in a living context, so the different media are usefully complementary. You are certainly right that not all such drawings are equally good; some of the very old ones are interesting historically but are too coarse to be useful botanically.

: The illustrations in Köhler's 1897 ''Medicinal Plants'' on the other hand are extremely clear and accurate, down to microscopic detail: his ''Picea abies'' includes a pollen grain and a cross-section of a needle leaf, for instance, as well as details of the seeds and cone scales. 

: As Köhler's title states, his drawings are directly relevant to an understanding of the uses of [[medicinal plants|plants as medicines]], which is definitely encyclopedic. 

: Early botanical illustrations of a species are in addition of interest as part of the history of study of a species, something that clearly makes them encyclopedic and worthy of inclusion. 

: For all these reasons, (and I haven't even mentioned their beauty and artistic value) I'd say that good botanical illustrations like Köhler's are undoubtedly of value to Wikipedia's plant articles. : Yes, the use of CiteHighlighter is at best a guide; blind usage of the tool (of any tool) is dangerous. 

: A specific issue is that you are removing what everyone up to now has taken to be reliable sources, leaving nothing but an uncited claim. You need to replace the removed citation (if you are *sure* the source is unusable) with a citation needed tag, so that other editors who know the subject matter of the article can repair the damage. Otherwise, what you are doing, much of the time, is making it look as if a later citation is covering the now-uncited claim, when it isn't. 

: i.e.  there was:   .......claim 1,[1] and claim 2.[2] 

: you convert this to:    .......claim 1, and claim 2.[2] 

: which appears to visitors as if claim 1 is cited to [2], which is an error, amounting to abuse of sources.

: Could you therefore please take care not to remove sources unless *absolutely* necessary, and to insert a citation needed tag in the exact same place. Thank you. [[User:Chiswick Chap|Chiswick Chap]] ([[User talk:Chiswick Chap|talk]]) 18:36, 21 October 2026 (UTC)

This model contradicts the earlier [[Bindu (symbol)|Bindu]] model in the same text.<ref name="Mallinson Singleton 2017"/><]] According to the 11th-12th century ''[[Gorakṣaśataka]]'', or "Hundred Verses of Goraksa", [[hatha yoga]] practices such as the mudras [[mula bandha]], uddiyana bandha, and [[Jalandhara Bandha|jalandhara bandha]], and the [[pranayama]] practice of [[kumbhaka]] can awaken Kundalini.<ref name="White 2012">{{cite book |last=White |first=David Gordon |author-link=David Gordon White |title=Yoga in Practice |date=2012 |publisher=Princeton University Press |location=Princeton, New Jersey |isbn=978-0-691-14085-8 |pages=2, 268–270}}</ref> Another hatha yoga text, the ''[[Khecarīvidyā]]'', states that [[khechari mudra]] enables one to raise Kundalini and access the stores of [[amrita]] in the head, which subsequently flood the body.<ref name="Mallinson3">{{cite book |last1=Mallinson |first1=James |author-link=James Mallinson (author) |title=The Khecarividya of Adinatha: A Critical Edition and Annotated Translation of an Early Text of Hathayoga |date=2007 |publisher=[[Routledge]] |location=London |isbn=978-0-415-39115-3 |page=29}}</ref> The concept of Kundalini is described in the ''[[Yoga-Kundalini Upanishad]]'', a <!--c. -->sixteenth century text.<ref>{{cite book |last=Larson |first=Gerald James |author-link=Gerald James Larson |title=The Encyclopedia of Indian Philosophies: India's Philosophy of Meditation |date=2008 The Encyclopedia of Indian Philosophies: Yoga: India's philosophy of meditation |publisher=[[Motilal Banarsidass]] |isbn=978-81-208-3349-4 |pages=476, 615–617}}</ref> The ''[[Hatha Yoga Pradipika]]'' presents two conflicting models of Hatha Yoga. Jung |date=1996 |location=Princeton, New Jersey |publisher=[[Princeton University Press]] |isbn=978-0-691-02127-0 |pages=xviii-xix, xxvi}}</ref> In the introduction to her edited version of Jung's seminar, [[Sonu Shamdasani]] wrote that [[depth psychology]] developed at the same time as Western awareness of yoga texts, as psychoanalysts sought to break free from the confines of Western thought.<ref name="Jung Shamdasani 1999"/> Reviewing the book, Davi Nichol commented that the seminar {{Blockquote|text="was widely regarded as a milestone in the psychological understanding of Eastern thought and of the symbolic transformations of inner experience. Kundalini yoga presented Jung with a model for the developmental phases of higher consciousness, and he interpreted its symbols in terms of the process of [[Individuation#Carl_Jung|individuation]], with sensitivity towards a new generation's interest in alternative religions and psychological exploration."<ref name="Nichol 1996">{{cite journal |last=Nichol |first=Davi |title=Book Review: ''The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga: Notes of the Seminar Given in 1932 by C.G. Jung'' (Princeton University Press, 1996) |journal=Psychoanalytic Books: A Quarterly Journal of Reviews |issue=10 |date=1999}}</ref>}} According to Jung, "the concept of Kundalini has for us only one use, that is, to describe our own experiences with the unconscious."<ref name="Hayman">{{cite book |last=Hayman |first=Ronald |title=A Life of Jung |date=2001 |publisher=[[W. W. Norton & Company|W. W. Norton]] |location=New York |isbn=978-0-393-32322-1 |page=[https://archive.org/details/lifeofjung00haym/page/304 304] |url=https://archive.org/details/lifeofjung00haym |url-access=registration |quote=the concept of Kundalini has for us only one use ...}}</ref> Jung used the Kundalini system symbolically as a means of understanding the dynamic movement between conscious and unconscious processes.<ref name="Jung Shamdasani 1999"/> According to Shamdasani, Jung claimed that the symbolism of Kuṇḍalinī yoga suggested that the bizarre symptomatology that patients at times presented, actually resulted from the awakening of the Kuṇḍalinī. He argued that knowledge of such symbolism enabled much that would otherwise be seen as the meaningless by-products of a disease process to be understood as meaningful symbolic processes, and explicated the often peculiar physical localizations of symptoms.<ref name="Jung Shamdasani 1999"/> The popularization of eastern spiritual practices has been associated with psychological problems in the west. [[Psychiatry|Psychiatric]] literature states that "since the influx of eastern spiritual practices and the rising popularity of meditation starting in the 1960s, many people have experienced a variety of psychological difficulties, either while engaged in intensive spiritual practice or spontaneously."<ref name="Turner 1995">{{cite journal |last1=Turner |first1=R. P. |last2=Lukoff |first2=D. |last3=Barnhouse |first3=R. T. |last4=Lu |first4=F. G. |title=Religious or spiritual problem. A culturally sensitive diagnostic category in the DSM-IV |journal=[[The Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease]] |date=July 1995 |volume=183 |issue=7 |pages=435–444 |doi=10.1097/00005053-199507000-00003 |pmid=7623015}}</ref> Among the psychological difficulties associated with intensive spiritual practice we find "Kundalini awakening," "a complex physio-psychospiritual transformative process described in the yogic tradition."<ref name="Turner 1995"/> Researchers in [[transpersonal psychology]]<ref name="Scotton 1999"/> have described a complex pattern of sensory, motor, mental, and affective symptoms associated with the concept of Kundalini, sometimes called the Kundalini syndrome.<ref name="Greyson 1993">{{cite journal |last=Greyson |first=Bruce |title=Near-death experiences and the physio-kundalini syndrome |journal=[[Journal of Religion & Health]] |date=1993 |volume=32 |issue=4 |pages=277–290 |doi=10.1007/BF00990954 |pmid=24271550}}</ref> Spiritual emergency associated with Kuṇḍalinī awakening may be viewed as an acute [[psychotic episode]] by psychiatrists who are not conversant with the culture. The biological changes of increased [[P300 (neuroscience)|P300]] amplitudes that occur with certain yogic practices may lead to acute psychosis. Biological alterations by Yogic techniques may be used to warn people against such reactions.<ref name="Bharadwaj 2012">{{cite journal |last=Bharadwaj |first=Balaji |title=Proof-of-concept studies in Yoga and mental health |journal=International Journal of Yoga |date=2012 |volume=5 |issue=1 |page=74 |doi=10.4103/0973-6131.91719 |doi-broken-date=8 November 2026 |pmc=3276938 |pmid=22346071 |doi-access=free }}</ref> ===] Aurobindo === [[Sri Aurobindo]] (1872…

Jung'' (Princeton University Press, 1996) |journal=Psychoanalytic Books: A Quarterly Journal of Reviews |issue=10 |date=1999}}</ref>}} According to Jung, "the concept of Kundalini has for us only one use, that is, to describe our own experiences with the unconscious."<ref name="Hayman">{{cite book |last=Hayman |first=Ronald |title=A Life of Jung |date=2001 |publisher=[[W. W. Norton & Company|W. W. Norton]] |location=New York |isbn=978-0-393-32322-1 |page=[https://archive.org/details/lifeofjung00haym/page/304 304] |url=https://archive.org/details/lifeofjung00haym |url-access=registration |quote=the concept of Kundalini has for us only one use ...}}</ref> Jung used the Kundalini system symbolically as a means of understanding the dynamic movement between conscious and unconscious processes.<ref name="Jung Shamdasani 1999"/> According to Shamdasani, Jung claimed that the symbolism of Kuṇḍalinī yoga suggested that the bizarre symptomatology that patients at times presented, actually resulted from the awakening of the Kuṇḍalinī. He argued that knowledge of such symbolism enabled much that would otherwise be seen as the meaningless by-products of a disease process to be understood as meaningful symbolic processes, and explicated the often peculiar physical localizations of symptoms.<ref name="Jung Shamdasani 1999"/> The popularization of eastern spiritual practices has been associated with psychological problems in the west. Psychiatric literature states that "since the influx of eastern spiritual practices and the rising popularity of meditation starting in the 1960s, many people have experienced a variety of psychological difficulties, either while engaged in intensive spiritual practice or spontaneously."<ref name="Turner 1995">{{cite journal |last1=Turner |first1=R. P. |last2=Lukoff |first2=D. |last3=Barnhouse |first3=R. T. |last4=Lu |first4=F. G. |title=Religious or spiritual problem. A culturally sensitive diagnostic category in the DSM-IV |journal=[[The Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease]] |date=July 1995 |volume=183 |issue=7 |pages=435–444 |doi=10.1097/00005053-199507000-00003 |pmid=7623015}}</ref> Among the psychological difficulties associated with intensive spiritual practice we find "Kundalini awakening," "a complex physio-psychospiritual transformative process described in the yogic tradition."<ref name="Turner 1995"/> Researchers in [[transpersonal psychology]]<ref name="Scotton 1999"/> have described a complex pattern of sensory, motor, mental, and affective symptoms associated with the concept of Kundalini, sometimes called the Kundalini syndrome.<ref name="Greyson 1993">{{cite journal |last=Greyson |first=Bruce |title=Near-death experiences and the physio-kundalini syndrome |journal=[[Journal of Religion & Health]] |date=1993 |volume=32 |issue=4 |pages=277–290 |doi=10.1007/BF00990954 |pmid=24271550}}</ref> Spiritual emergency associated with Kuṇḍalinī awakening may be viewed as an acute [[psychotic episode]] by psychiatrists who are not conversant with the culture. The biological changes of increased [[P300 (neuroscience)|P300]] amplitudes that occur with certain yogic practices may lead to acute psychosis. Biological alterations by Yogic techniques may be used to warn people against such reactions.<ref name="Bharadwaj 2012">{{cite journal |last=Bharadwaj |first=Balaji |title=Proof-of-concept studies in and mental health |journal=International Journal of Yoga |date=2012 |volume=5 |issue=1 |page=74 |doi=10.4103/0973-6131.91719 |doi-broken-date=8 |pmc=3276938 |pmid=22346071 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Certain species consume [[worm]]s or [[insect]]s and carrion in their normal habitats. Too much protein is detrimental in herbivorous species, and has been associated with shell deformities and other medical problems. Different tortoise species vary greatly in their nutritional requirements. Behavior Communication in tortoises is different from many other reptiles. Because they are restricted by their shell and short limbs, [[visual communication]] is not a strong form of communication in tortoises. Tortoises use [[Olfaction|olfactory cues]] to determine the sex of other tortoises so that they can find a potential mate. [[Haptic communication|Tactile communication]] is important in tortoises during combat and courtship.
