items.post_text:
=== Comments ===

* <s>The article, although short, embodies quite a serious problem of structure as all 3 of the main sections (i.e. barring the 'History') contain discussions of the same issue, namely slippage and failure with certain types of line or rope:
::: 'Properties': no good for HMPE/dyneema/nylon monofilament; remedy = more turns (triple knot?)
::: 'Uses': no good for HMPE/aramid; remedy = triple knot
::: 'Security': no good for ([[Kernmantle rope]]s) Spectra/Technora cores; remedy = triple knot
: Clearly these need to be discussed in one section, i.e. the body of the article needs to be restructured from the existing 3-section (post-History) arrangement.</s>
:::: I've rearranged the article to only have two sections after the history section. The 'security' section was moved to 'properties' and I took a sentence about slippage out of the 'uses' section.

* <s>In 'Properties', the issue of untying/jamming when tightened is mentioned in both paragraphs before sliding (if that's the word) into related matters. This needs rewriting to make each point once in an orderly way.</s>
::If that is intended as a pun, its very subtle, I appreciate it. I've reworked the section quite a bit with the merge of material from the other two sections.

* <s>The aside {{tq|(cordelette)}} needs to be explained with its climbing context and properly integrated in the text; an illustration would make sense here to show what the term means and how the knot functions in this situation.</s>
:: I've added a picture and more of an explanation of what cordalettes are used for with a wikilink.

* <s>The use of three similar and somewhat repetitive infoboxes is undesirable; the information so presented would be better in a comparative table to avoid repetition, not to mention the lengthy use of screen real-estate down the side of a large part of the text. Really there should be at most 1 infobox, specially as it's agreed they are all closely related (or the merge would have been a mistake).</s>
::Yeah, when I did the merge and expanded the article I struggled with this. I've made it one infobox and I'll consider adding a comparison table to the end of the article (maybe with a gallery of other pictures from commons as well).
::: Sounds promising! 

* <s>'grapevine knot' is uncited; 'new' claims should not in any case be introduced in the lead section. 
The other alternative names are cited but the ref and the claims should be moved from lead to the article body.</s>
::That name is also in Ashley's book of Knots, I'll clarify and move everything to the history section.
:::Should be done now.

* <s>'reliability' is mentioned only in the lead; the claim should be introduced in the article body and the citation moved out of the lead.</s>
::I've rephrased it to just strength and added a line on it in the body with a note discussing what the sources mean by "strength".

* <s>'search and rescue' is mentioned only in the lead; the claim should be introduced in the article body and properly explained (are there considerations there different from climbing, for example? are there S&R applications where untying is not necessary? - seems surprising) and the citation moved out of the lead.</s>
:: I've added a sentence and a source to the uses section.

* <s>{{tq|The technique used in tying the knot is important to determining the behavior of the knot under load.}} This 'Security' claim is not explained so it comes across as mysterious; the only clue (on re-reading) is the oblique mention {{tq|the initial geometry}}: but two obscure claims don't add up to clarity.</s>
::I've reworked the paragraph, is it clearer now?
::: Much improved. 

* <s>'Uses' should have a paragraph on surgical usage, as currently the only mention is from Classical times.</s>
::Done, added three new sources.</s>
::: Feels much more complete now.

* <s>'[[Manila rope]]' should be wikilinked (with uppercase M).</s>
::Done

* <s>Insufficient use has been made of [1] Tong 2024, in particular of how the geometry of the knot changes during tightening with the two strangle knots moving together and apart.</s>
:: Added additional paragraph on the various behaviors of the knot under load.
::: Super.

* <s>[7] describes another use, 'handfasting' during a wedding. Should be in 'Uses'.</s>
::Done, with another note on it from abok.

== Images ==

* All three images are on Commons, are relevant, and suitably licensed.
::The images I've added are also all on commons
== Sources ==

* <s>Refs [2] and [3] need page numbers.</s>
::Done, I've added page numbers to the entire source, do you want me to add notes for specific citations? For example for the history section?
* <s>Ref [6] is to YouTube, and a commercial source there at that: both fail to meet [[WP:RS]].</s>
::Removed, the claim is also backed up by other sources, including source [3]
* <s>The page refs in the infobox to "''[[ABoK]]''" ([2] in the reflist, actually) need to be related to the text in some way, ideally by using them in sfn refs within the source. I understand that knot articles have historically used this curious shorthand but as it's not a general form of citation per [[WP:CITE]], and doesn't match the citation style in use in the article, some integration is required.</s>
::I added page numbers to the ABoK source where the names are listed (in the history section now). Those pages also list the ABoK numbers. Or do you think the sfn refs are necessary in the infobox itself?
::: Much improved. Since the infobox style seems to be standard for knots, we'd best leave it alone, however odd it looks.
* <s>[1] ok, though "its strength and reliability" is copied directly from the source.</s>
::I'm pretty sure I didn't copy it, but I do see that its in the abstract, I'll try to rephrase (not sure how, there's only so many ways of saying that).
* <s>[2] page needed.</s>
::Added to source, let me know if I should add notes with exact page numbers.

::Added to source, let me know if I should add notes with exact page numbers. From pages 123 & 124 {{tq|Many peoples, apparently independently from each other, have come across this loop knot. The two knots}} (meaning the fisherman's in a loop and the fisherman's in a bend) {{tq|are structurally equivalent, though they differ in functionality. However, knowledge of the loop knot version may well imply familiarity with the structure as a bend.}} (...) {{tq|However, as said, it is not possible to make a join reminiscent of a rawhide splice in baleen. == Bringing some order to Kundalini-related articles ==

I've taken a tour around Wikipedia's Kundalini-related articles (including [[Prana]], [[Pranayama]], [[Chakra]], and so forth), and have found it quite disordered. Major texts were barely mentioned; citations were haphazard and often incomplete; illustrations were patchy; explanations were sketchy, missing, or contradictory; Wiki-voice was used for the opinion of one modern yoga school, or one particular medieval text, but not for others; dates were largely absent; and the articles neither flowed logically, nor matched what was at the other end of many of the provided wikilinks. 

Accordingly, I'm working to improve the clarity and reliability of our coverage of these topics. I've added timelines, diagrams, and photographs; documented gurus with their dates; filled in many citations; reduced overlaps; added explanations and sources; and paraphrased several very lengthy quotations. This remains a work-in-progress, but I hope editors will find the articles somewhat more approachable already. Any assistance in improving the articles further will be warmly welcomed. 

One specific issue is that this article, [[Kundalini Yoga]] (an evidently ambiguous title), overlaps markedly with the [[Kundalini]] article. It could be argued that any yoga practice which acknowledges Kundalini (certainly from the time of the ''Hatha Yoga Pradipika'', and possibly earlier) could be called 'Kundalini Yoga', while more recently, multiple yoga gurus have taught something called 'Kundalini Yoga' but incorporating their own selection of beliefs and practices. This means that it is not clear what we should have in an article entitled "[[Kundalini Yoga]]" that is not in the Kundalini article. 

It would be possible to create several subsidiary articles on subtopics such as [[Kundalini Yoga (Yogi Bhajan)]], [[Kundalini Yoga (Guru Jagat)]], [[Kundalini Yoga (Sri Aurobindo)]], and so on, but it is not clear that this would be practical or (given the mainly primary sourcing for each such variant), actually encyclopedic. I suggest therefore that for the moment we simply merge [[Kundalini Yoga]] into [[Kundalini]]: or rather, make it a redirect, as the two articles already substantially overlapped, and after the work I've done to clarify, fill out, and organise the Kundalini article, it basically covers both the pre-modern and the modern history and concepts, so it spans the various meanings of 'Kundalini Yoga' in the wider context of an explanation of Kundalini itself. 

To get things into a consistent state, I'll make this a redirect now, and will have a think about which articles it would be desirable to create to make the topic area clearer. One such is ''[[The Serpent Power (book)]]'', on the 1919 book by 'Arthur Avalon'. No doubt you will have further ideas for new articles. [[User:Chiswick Chap|Chiswick Chap]] ([[User talk:Chiswick Chap|talk]]) 15:47, 5 November 2026 (UTC)

== Medical-sounding claims not from a [[Systematic review]]; [[WP:OR|Original research]] ==

An editor has now repeatedly attempted to get some material on the medical-sounding topic "Connective tissue physiology" into the article as a top-level chapter, supported initially by [[WP:PRIMARY]] sources which are plainly not sufficient to meet [[WP:MEDRS]]. The material was then reworked with medical language and reinserted cited to an article in ''[[Physical Therapy journal|Physical therapy]]''. I would not like to say whether that journal is appropriate for any sort of medical-sounding claim. 

In addition, half of the material was uncited, reading like [[WP:OR|Original Research]], the editor's personal interpretation. The source cited is paywalled, but a search does not support the presence of "Yin Yoga" in that source: if indeed it is not mentioned there (and there is no hint of it in the abstract) then this is pure editorial, which is forbidden on Wikipedia. To be clear, policy specifically forbids the making of any inference, however simple it may appear, from what a source says (about a piece of research, say) to what it might possibly mean in the world (such as when yoga is practised). 

A further serious issue is that claims are being made for the effectiveness of a practice without [[Systematic review]] which is not just any kind of review: it is a systematic analysis of the quality of the evidence (such as it may be) presented by researchers in the field, with conclusions about whether the claims can be sustained strongly, weakly, or not at all. Such a systematic review rejects evidence that is from informal trials or experiments that lack a proper [[Treatment and control groups|control group in their experimental design]]; and it is likely that it would challenge any evidence that is not secured with a [[Blinded experiment|double-blind controlled trial]], something that is difficult to achieve with a physical practice. 

For these reasons (either of which would be sufficient), I've deleted the material from the article. 

An additional point is that it is quite unacceptable for an editor to make repeated attempts to insert challenged material into an article. Once they are aware, because of a deletion and an edit comment, that material is challenged, the only options are discussion on the talk page or to drop the attempt: anything else is [[WP:DISRUPTIVE|disruptive editing]]. [[User:Chiswick Chap|Chiswick Chap]] ([[User talk:Chiswick Chap|talk]]) 08:45, 7 June 2026 (UTC)

== Variability alone is of no interest ==

An editor has now repeatedly added a claim about variability of leg length, with no explanation of why this may have arisen or what function it serves. Every species has a mass of alleles and phenotypic variability, which we cannot possibly document, nor should we: that's a task for genomic and other databases. In a general article, facts of that kind only surface to general interest level if they come with specific evidence of their evolutionary function: otherwise, they are just pointless and useless clutter which make general readers wonder why they are reading such stuff. == [[PNAS]] paper by Margulis et al is mainstream science ==

An editor has seen fit to try to remove a brief mention of a research article in [[PNAS]] in 2006, asserting it's "fringe". However, PNAS is a (highly) respected mainstream journal with a robust scientific peer-review process. Now it may well be that the paper's proposal is incorrect: science goes like that. The appropriate response for mainstream science mistakes, if such it be, is not editorial censorship ("we know best"), but the addition of later sources that question or refute the proposal made. Since "once notable, always notable" is a correct Wiki-slogan, we do not go about deleting relevant accounts of an idea's history; instead, we update them from the latest sources. :Hi, I'm sorry to hear that the article seems biased to you, and your clear explanation of the issue is very welcome. However, it would, I think, be difficult to remove all the non-English names from the article, as it would risk becoming incomprehensible, and I suspect it would look and feel very strange, rather like writing about French cuisine with no French words present. Hindi is just one of multiple languages printed on Indian banknotes, so it certainly can't claim universality. What to do about that here, if anything, is more challenging. I note that we already have words in a variety of languages including Bhojpuri, Kashmiri, and Marathi; further, quite a few of the terms used, such as pilau, biryani, dal, kebab, ghee, tandoori, and rogan josh are familiar in British usage and probably more widely in other varieties of English also. Some other words like dahi could be translated as 'yogurt', though that carries connotations such as being commercially prepared and packed which would be wrong in the context; the translation 'curd' is more accurate, but the word is Indian English and not really familiar to a broader audience, though [[Little Miss Muffet]]'s "eating her curds and whey" might possibly suggest roughly the right meaning to some readers. All of this is to say, that removing the non-English names, while possibly desirable, might not be the best approach. I think it might perhaps be better to consider adding some names from other languages to increase diversity and balance somewhat. 
:It would be interesting to know what other editors feel about this, and what they think should best be done about it. [[User:Chiswick Chap|Chiswick Chap]] ([[User talk:Chiswick Chap|talk]]) 19:39, 2 November 2026 (UTC)

::The semantics of "followed_by/preceded_by" are ambiguous. For an author who writes separate novels, one per year, they mean "next year's/last year's novel" with no implication that the novels are about the same characters, situation, or plot. For a book series, the semantics suddenly become limited to the series, so "the next/previous volume in this particular series". I dare say that for an author who writes some novels and some poetry, the semantics permit "next/previous novel" for the one and "next/previous collection of poetry" for the other. 
:: In this case, I think it is sufficient to note that the infobox already has "'''|series = Stand-alone'''", i.e. it is clearly indicated that the context here is a stand-alone novel, so there can be no doubt that the following book is a separate novel. items.post_text: :All the parthenogenetic offspring's alleles come from the mother. An allele is a form of a specific gene. Say there are 2 alleles of two genes (A and B). The mother is heterozygous for one gene, Aa (with two alleles), and homozygous for the other, BB (with one allele). The offspring could be AABB or aaBB, both of which mean it has less allele diversity than its mother. You can see that if the mother was heterozygous for a lot of genes, the offspring are likely to have close to half her alleles; if she was homozygous for all of them, the offspring must have all her alleles. [[User:Chiswick Chap|Chiswick Chap]] ([[User talk:Chiswick Chap|talk]]) 07:58, 8 October 2026 (UTC)

== The Yoga family of articles ==

Hi, I noticed your edit to [[Yoga]]. That article is unsurprisingly at the head of a large family of articles, covering branches of classical, hatha, and modern yogas and a wide range of related topics, including many asanas and social issues. These last cover topics such as commercialisation, politics, and cultural appropriation. There is thus a hierarchy [[Yoga]] - [[Modern yoga]] - [[Yoga as exercise]] - [[Yoga in society]] - ... all the society topics ... so appropriation is no fewer than 4 levels down the tree (for instance, there are some 200 Yoga as exercise articles, not counting [[Asana]]s). You'll appreciate that each of these many articles has to be written neutrally, explaining the various points of view ([[WP:NPOV]]) making use of reliable sources ([[WP:RS]]) on its particular topic. Appropriation is a sensitive topic and widely differing opinions have been expressed on it; there isn't room up at the top of the tree to do it justice, nor to cover the various sources appropriately. I've therefore undone your edit to Yoga, but thought it would be helpful to let you know the context, and that the topic has in fact been covered in detail already. Hi, please don't add 'new' materials or citations to the lead of any properly-constructed Wikipedia article.

I see you're in your first 1,000 edits, so I hope you won't mind if I just run over the principles, apologies if you know most of it already.

* The lead is a summary, normally without repeating the citations, of the article body, which should be fully cited.

* Citations are repeated from the body to the lead only in special situations, such as highly inflammatory topics (as with articles on countries that are at war, that sort of thing). That text must of course be cited (remedially, if it's an old uncited article). Best, if editing such a thing, is immediately to create section headings and add a brief summary as a new lead section.

:On the use of Quenya in Wikipedia, I think we have to be careful to stay within the real world rather than going in-universe. I recognise that there are thousands of lovers of artificial language, and thousands more Tolkien fans, who would like to include every minute detail of Quenya grammar. But for Joe M. Public (Wikipedia reader), even the word "Noldor" is at the limit of comprehensibility, and if understood at all, Joe will very likely read it as synonymous with "Elves" or indeed with "some group or other of Tolkien characters". The word "Noldo", especially if used exactly once, will be taken as either a typographic error for "Noldor", or an obscure bit of language of uncertain meaning, inserted by an overenthusiastic Tolkien fan. In short, we should not wish to go there on Wikipedia. I've adjusted the grammar to avoid any perceived need for "Noldo" (even if we were following Quenya grammar).
:On the use of the formal register of English, we need to consider whether formality is actually required in Wikipedia articles. English Wikipedia is unique in that it is widely consulted by people whose native language is not English. Compare Finnish or Swedish Wikis, for example, and you will appreciate that we editors of the English Wiki have to write not just for a public that wants a quick, simple overview of a topic, but who need it in very plain English. For me, that means that formal, stiff, old-fashioned, and wordy written-only registers of English are inappropriate. Policy tells us to avoid contractions like "can't" and "it's", so we spell those out; but equally, we avoid "heretofore", "moreover", "therewith", and I'm afraid "whom" as unnecessarily difficult. "Correctness" is, you will find, remarkably hard to define, as there are many "correct" forms of English. Dictionaries such as the OED take care to explain that they do not dictate correctness, but instead describe native-speaker usage. For me, the correct register for Wikipedia is simple, plain, uncontracted, and avoids needless grammatical complexity. There you have it. All the best, [[User:Chiswick Chap|Chiswick Chap]] ([[User talk:Chiswick Chap#top|talk]]) 07:26, 8 July 2026 (UTC)

: Hi Chilicave, I'll see what I can do. 

The first thing I'd say at a casual glance is that if you'd told me it was a GA and you were working it up to FA, I'd not have been surprised; it looks to be in a reasonable state. So, getting it to GA shouldn't be too hard, I hope. 

If you're not familiar with the 6 GA criteria, you should make their acquaintance. The key questions are does it cover the main points of its subject, and is it reliably sourced throughout. The "main points" question requires some knowledge of the subject to answer; my guess is "yes" but the "Types" section does look a bit thin. The sources look suitable at a first glance. 

Some more detailed comments: 

=== Sources ===

The 'Sources' list covers some but not all of the books cited, which looks untidy. It would be best to move all the books there and to link to them (all) using the mechanism <nowiki>{{sfn|Boyce|1975|pp=147–191}}</nowiki> and so on. 

=== References ===

The references are uneven in multiple ways. To give a few examples among many:
* [8] Nigal, p. 81. lacks date (and should use the sfn template as above)
* [9] Drower, 1944:78 uses a non-standard format for page.
* [16] Hume again lacks date; there are many other examples.
* You sometimes have "pages", sometimes "P.", sometimes "p./pp.", and sometimes the pages are missing altogether (e.g. [44] Sinha 2008). 
* [39] bizarrely says "ISBN" but does not provide one. ISBN is actually optional, but if you're providing them for books then all the books should have them (or an OCLC if there is no ISBN for early books). 
* [43] Prinja 2009 does not correctly provide either the article title ("Weddings") nor the publisher ("BBC").
* Authors are sometimes given as Bloggs, Joe M.; sometimes as Joe M. Bloggs; and sometimes as Bloggs JM. I suggest we always use |last=Bloggs |first=Joe M. in the <nowiki>{{cite book |last= ...}}</nowiki> or equivalent template. 

=== Text ===

Suggest you move all the citations out of the lead; I notice that [1], [3], and [4] occur only in the lead, which is an error: everything in the lead should already be discussed and cited in the article body. That means that the lead should say nothing "new": if it's cited, that claim and citation are in the wrong place; if it's uncited, it's in the wrong place and is possibly [[WP:OR]] as well.

Once you've done that and tidied up the article body, revisit the lead and ensure it provides a coherent summary of the article's main points.

Agni is sometimes in italics, sometimes in roman.

All the texts named should be in italics.

In 'Upanishads', I suggest we have a transliteration into Latin characters (or IAST) beside the Devanagari text, with the translation beneath it. The existing "translation" is actually heavily interpreted, an "unpacking" translation at best, as immediately evidenced by its inordinate length: if we were to use such a thing, the interpretation would need to be reliably sourced, so I suspect it's unusable as it stands. Google Translate offers a transliteration and a direct translation:

<poem>ath yadyagnya ityachakshate bramacharyamev 
tadbramacharyen hyev yo dnyata tam 
vindate̕th yadishtamityachakshate bramacharyamev 
tadbramacharyen hyeveshtvatmanamanuvindate</poem>

<poem>Then if they call it sacrifice, it is celibacy 
That is the one who is known by celibacy
Then he finds what he desires, and they call it celibacy 
That, by celibacy, he worships and attains to himself</poem>

"Tadeusz Skorupski states" - who's he? We try to gloss and wikilink attributed authorities.

Why do "yagam" and "yagnam" redirect here? They're not found anywhere in the article, so either they should be added (and cited) in the text, or the hatnotes and the redirects should be deleted. 

Having the incomprehensibly [[Delphic ambiguity|Delphic]] hatnote "For concurrent Hindu usage, see [[Homa (ritual)]]" is not satisfactory, as there is plainly some relationship between the two things, and that relationship needs to be explained in a paragraph of cited text (maybe even a whole section called '== Ritual context ==' or something of that kind). Something important seems to be missing there.

'Types' first paragraph introduces several terms, but never explains any of them except śrauta  (which it links only later, and spells it differently). If the types are worth introducing then they must be clearly explained and differentiated (what are they and how/when are they each used?). The second paragraph partially explains "srauta" with an interpolation of yet another type not mentioned in the first paragraph, "Grhya" in the middle before the text returns to srauta again. The whole section needs to be rewritten for the average Wikipedia reader (Joe M. Public): Joe has heard of Hinduism and supposes it is quite like Buddhism, but never heard of yajna let alone of its subtypes. (I suspect Joe would have quite a lot of trouble with most of the other sections.)

'Method' mentions obliquely that the altar is "set in a mandapa or mandala or kundam," and the next sentence mentions that this encompasses a "square principle". The *very* determined reader can discover by searching for [[mandala]] that such things are square ... a link and an explanation are needed.

=== See also ===

Remove "yasna" as it's already discussed and linked in the text. Also "vedi"; maybe others.

=== Images ===

Diagrams must be big enough to be readable; the sacrificial space diagram was too small so I've adjusted it, but it needs redrawing with larger text labels (should be made in PowerPoint and saved to an SVG file, then uploaded to Commons), as even enlarged the text is very tiny.

The other images mostly seem relevant and well-chosen; they are on Commons and are plausibly licensed. The exception is "A miniature illustration of a falcon bird Athirathram yajna altar built using the square principle" which is uncited and not explained in the text. (Oh, "falcon bird" and "square principle" are mentioned higher up in the text, see 'Text' above, but it's really scrappy, and the bird's name is not mentioned or cited at all.) If it's relevant it needs to be explained a good deal more (why a falcon? who's Athirathram? what's the square principle? etc) and cited in a paragraph of text; if not, delete it.

The pair of images in 'Types' is headed "Different types of yajna" but it does not say what types they are, so it's unhelpful. The left image says its "Vedic" but it seems that applies to all yajnas? The other one has no hint of its type at all (and the image quality is, ahem, dreadful).

=== Summary ===

As always, the devil is in the detail. The article makes a worthy attempt at the subject, but in detail it is not coherent, not easy to follow, and does not seem to cover the topic; whether it covers the "main points" is not easy to ascertain. : Hi Chilicave, I'll see what I can do. 

The first thing I'd say at a casual glance is that if you'd told me it was a GA and you were working it up to FA, I'd not have been surprised; it looks to be in a reasonable state. So, getting it to GA shouldn't be too hard, I hope. 

If you're not familiar with the 6 GA criteria, you should make their acquaintance. The key questions are does it cover the main points of its subject, and is it reliably sourced throughout. The "main points" question requires some knowledge of the subject to answer; my guess is "yes" but the "Types" section does look a bit thin. The sources look suitable at a first glance. 

Some more detailed comments: 

=== Sources ===

The 'Sources' list covers some but not all of the books cited, which looks untidy. It would be best to move all the books there and to link to them (all) using the mechanism <nowiki>{{sfn|Boyce|1975|pp=147–191}}</nowiki> and so on. 

=== References ===

The references are uneven in multiple ways. To give a few examples among many:
* [8] Nigal, p. 81. lacks date (and should use the sfn template as above)
* [9] Drower, 1944:78 uses a non-standard format for page.
* [16] Hume again lacks date; there are many other examples.
* You sometimes have "pages", sometimes "P.", sometimes "p./pp.", and sometimes the pages are missing altogether (e.g. [44] Sinha 2008). 
* [39] bizarrely says "ISBN" but does not provide one. ISBN is actually optional, but if you're providing them for books then all the books should have them (or an OCLC if there is no ISBN for early books). 
* [43] Prinja 2009 does not correctly provide either the article title ("Weddings") nor the publisher ("BBC").
* Authors are sometimes given as Bloggs, Joe M.; sometimes as Joe M. Bloggs; and sometimes as Bloggs JM. I suggest we always use |last=Bloggs |first=Joe M. in the <nowiki>{{cite book |last= ...}}</nowiki> or equivalent template. 

=== Text ===

Suggest you move all the citations out of the lead; I notice that [1], [3], and [4] occur only in the lead, which is an error: everything in the lead should already be discussed and cited in the article body. That means that the lead should say nothing "new": if it's cited, that claim and citation are in the wrong place; if it's uncited, it's in the wrong place and is possibly [[WP:OR]] as well.

Once you've done that and tidied up the article body, revisit the lead and ensure it provides a coherent summary of the article's main points.

Agni is sometimes in italics, sometimes in roman.

All the texts named should be in italics.

In 'Upanishads', I suggest we have a transliteration into Latin characters (or IAST) beside the Devanagari text, with the translation beneath it. The existing "translation" is actually heavily interpreted, an "unpacking" translation at best, as immediately evidenced by its inordinate length: if we were to use such a thing, the interpretation would need to be reliably sourced, so I suspect it's unusable as it stands. Google Translate offers a transliteration and a direct translation:

<poem>ath yadyagnya ityachakshate bramacharyamev 
tadbramacharyen hyev yo dnyata tam 
vindate̕th yadishtamityachakshate bramacharyamev 
tadbramacharyen hyeveshtvatmanamanuvindate</poem>

<poem>Then if they call it sacrifice, it is celibacy 
That is the one who is known by celibacy
Then he finds what he desires, and they call it celibacy 
That, by celibacy, he worships and attains to himself</poem>

"Tadeusz Skorupski states" - who's he? We try to gloss and wikilink attributed authorities.

Why do "yagam" and "yagnam" redirect here? They're not found anywhere in the article, so either they should be added (and cited) in the text, or the hatnotes and the redirects should be deleted. 

Having the incomprehensibly [[Delphic ambiguity|Delphic]] hatnote "For concurrent Hindu usage, see [[Homa (ritual)]]" is not satisfactory, as there is plainly some relationship between the two things, and that relationship needs to be explained in a paragraph of cited text (maybe even a whole section called '== Ritual context ==' or something of that kind). Something important seems to be missing there.

'Types' first paragraph introduces several terms, but never explains any of them except śrauta  (which it links only later, and spells it differently). If the types are worth introducing then they must be clearly explained and differentiated (what are they and how/when are they each used?). The second paragraph partially explains "srauta" with an interpolation of yet another type not mentioned in the first paragraph, "Grhya" in the middle before the text returns to srauta again. The whole section needs to be rewritten for the average Wikipedia reader (Joe M. Public): Joe has heard of Hinduism and supposes it is quite like Buddhism, but never heard of yajna let alone of its subtypes. (I suspect Joe would have quite a lot of trouble with most of the other sections.)

'Method' mentions obliquely that the altar is "set in a mandapa or mandala or kundam," and the next sentence mentions that this encompasses a "square principle". The *very* determined reader can discover by searching for [[mandala]] that such things are square ... a link and an explanation are needed.

=== See also ===

Remove "yasna" as it's already discussed and linked in the text. Also "vedi"; maybe others.

=== Images ===

Diagrams must be big enough to be readable; the sacrificial space diagram was too small so I've adjusted it, but it needs redrawing with larger text labels (should be made in PowerPoint and saved to an SVG file, then uploaded to Commons), as even enlarged the text is very tiny.

The other images mostly seem relevant and well-chosen; they are on Commons and are plausibly licensed. The exception is "A miniature illustration of a falcon bird Athirathram yajna altar built using the square principle" which is uncited and not explained in the text. (Oh, "falcon bird" and "square principle" are mentioned higher up in the text, see 'Text' above, but it's really scrappy, and the bird's name is not mentioned or cited at all.) If it's relevant it needs to be explained a good deal more (why a falcon? who's Athirathram? what's the square principle? etc) and cited in a paragraph of text; if not, delete it.

The pair of images in 'Types' is headed "Different types of yajna" but it does not say what types they are, so it's unhelpful. The left image says its "Vedic" but it seems that applies to all yajnas? The other one has no hint of its type at all (and the image quality is, ahem, dreadful).

=== Summary ===

As always, the devil is in the detail. The article makes a worthy attempt at the subject, but in detail it is not coherent, not easy to follow, and does not seem to cover the topic; whether it covers the "main points" is not easy to ascertain. I suspect that quite a lot of rewriting will be necessary. Good luck! [[User:Chiswick Chap|Chiswick Chap]] ([[User talk:Chiswick Chap#top|talk]]) 09:28, 11 July 2026 (UTC)

Could I ask please that you work on it here (as you sort of implied above), and get it reviewed carefully (not just by me) before trying to add it again, as the repeated addition of raw un-Wiki-like material is fast becoming [[WP:DISRUPTIVE]]. Basically it would be best to attempt something much smaller (a single claim, a single citation, rather than a massive chunk of multiple sections). The reason for that is that there are many problems with: 

1) its structure, which should be with section and subsection headings using <nowiki>=== Section heading ===</nowiki> or <nowiki>==== Subsection heading ====</nowiki> as used here in this thread (but the article doesn't currently use subsections, so using them is basically deprecated).

2) its tone, which seems to be an editorial voice ("which appears to be a pure Nolan invention that is used 16 times in the movie." – which looks like pure "[[WP:OR|Original Research]]", forbidden on Wikipedia), not (as is required) a report of the views of scholars and critics (reliable secondary sources), nor even of Nolan (the primary source, to be used only in very small amounts, with caution and with direct attribution to page. This is a major and very serious problem with the current text, enough to have it immediately deleted even if all the other issues were fixed. 

3) its attempts at citations, which ought to be formatted using a template such as <nowiki>[[Template:Cite book]]</nowiki> complete with exact page number; other refs like <nowiki><ref>Various</ref></nowiki> are wholly unacceptable

4) formatting: we don't use boldface anywhere in articles except for the introductory phrase which reflects the article's name

5) the continued large amounts of uncited text.

6) the formatting of definitions as if this were a dictionary ([[WP:NOTDICT]]), or as if they were citations (they aren't)

7) the assembling of examples from primary sources to build up an argument, conveying an editorial opinion, is not allowed (Original Research by [[WP:SYNTH|Synthesis]]). This means that if you believe, say, that poem A and bible text B and literary text C all implicitly support conclusion D, that might be fine in a paper to a film society but is forbidden on Wikipedia. What you must do instead is to state that scholar S said that poem A is based on bible text B, and in S's stated view (which you might even quote) that means that conclusion D: but that requires you to find a suitable scholar S who actually wrote exactly that: you are not allowed to assemble the argument yourself, even if you believe the logic to be unassailable. Wikipedia, as an encyclopedia, is not a research platform, a news source, or a forum for arguing points of view. 

8) ... and so on. 

In other words, [[WP:CIR|a measure of Wiki-competence is required]], and the skill involved has many small components, all of which are unfortunately necessary to achieve an acceptable Wikitext. That can't be done in one giant leap, so it is necessary to learn in small steps. Hope this is clear, and sorry to bring what may seem like bad news. A good botanical drawing brings together all the key aspects of a plant needed for study and identification, something that is hard to achieve in a photograph – photos are good for showing individual features in a living context, so the different media are usefully complementary. Otherwise, what you are doing, much of the time, is making it look as if a later citation is covering the now-uncited claim, when it isn't. 

: i.e.  there was:   .......claim 1,[1] and claim 2.[2] 

: you convert this to:    .......claim 1, and claim 2.[2] 

: which appears to visitors as if claim 1 is cited to [2], which is an error, amounting to abuse of sources.

: Could you therefore please take care not to remove sources unless *absolutely* necessary, and to insert a citation needed tag in the exact same place. Thank you. [[User:Chiswick Chap|Chiswick Chap]] ([[User talk:Chiswick Chap|talk]]) 18:36, 21 October 2026 (UTC)

== Welcome! ==

Hello and [[Help:Introduction|welcome]] to Wikipedia!  I hope you like the place and decide to stay. Unfortunately, one or more of the articles you created, such as [[:Inundative application]], may not meet Wikipedia's [[Wikipedia:Core content policies|content policies]]. In short, to be included on Wikipedia, the topic of an article must be [[Wikipedia:Notability|notable]] and have been covered by published [[Wikipedia:Reliable sources|reliable]] and [[Wikipedia:Independent sources|independent sources]]. Articles must be written in a [[WP:NPOV|neutral manner]] and may not contain [[WP:NOLLM|AI generated material]].

Please read '''[[Help:Your first article|Your first article]]''' for an overview of the [[Wikipedia:Articles for creation|article creation process]]. The '''[[Wikipedia:Article wizard|Article Wizard]]''' is available to help you create an article for review. Note that articles are reviewed by volunteers and that it can take some time. If you'd like someone else to create an article, see [[Wikipedia:Requested articles|Requested articles]]. If you are stuck, come to the '''[[Wikipedia:Teahouse|Teahouse]]''', where experienced Wikipedians can help you through the processes.

New to Wikipedia? Please consider taking a look at [[Help:Introduction|our introductory tutorial]] or the page on [[Wikipedia:Contributing to Wikipedia|contributing to Wikipedia]]. Below are a few other good pages about article creation.
* [[Wikipedia:Article development|Article development]]
* [[Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Layout|Standard layout]]
* [[Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Lead section|Lead section]]
* [[Wikipedia:The perfect article|The perfect article]]
* [[Wikipedia:Task Center|Task Center]]{{snd}} for contributing to other articles. Writing a new article is tough, so getting experience elsewhere is useful.

I hope you enjoy editing here and being a [[Wikipedia:Wikipedians|Wikipedian]]! Please [[Wikipedia:Signatures|sign your name]] on talk pages using four tildes (<nowiki>~~~~</nowiki>); this will automatically produce your name and the date. If you have any questions, ask me on my talk page. You can also type '''{{tl|help me}}''' on this page, followed by your question, and someone will show up shortly to answer your questions. Again, welcome!<!-- Template:Welcome-first-article --> [[User:Chiswick Chap|Chiswick Chap]] ([[User talk:Chiswick Chap|talk]]) 11:02, 4 October 2026 (UTC)

kind.description: They review and improve articles on biology, yoga, literature, and food. They argue for complete coverage, clear explanations, focused sections, and introductions that summarize the main text. They check citations, image rights, and copied wording, basing judgments on published research, scholarly books, Wikipedia’s quality rules, and readability checks. They reject claims based on editors’ own knowledge or interpretations.

examples.post_text:
=== Comments ===

* <s>The article, although short, embodies quite a serious problem of structure as all 3 of the main sections (i.e. barring the 'History') contain discussions of the same issue, namely slippage and failure with certain types of line or rope:
::: 'Properties': no good for HMPE/dyneema/nylon monofilament; remedy = more turns (triple knot?)
::: 'Uses': no good for HMPE/aramid; remedy = triple knot
::: 'Security': no good for ([[Kernmantle rope]]s) Spectra/Technora cores; remedy = triple knot
: Clearly these need to be discussed in one section, i.e. the body of the article needs to be restructured from the existing 3-section (post-History) arrangement.</s>
:::: I've rearranged the article to only have two sections after the history section. The 'security' section was moved to 'properties' and I took a sentence about slippage out of the 'uses' section.

* <s>In 'Properties', the issue of untying/jamming when tightened is mentioned in both paragraphs before sliding (if that's the word) into related matters. This needs rewriting to make each point once in an orderly way.</s>
::If that is intended as a pun, its very subtle, I appreciate it. I've reworked the section quite a bit with the merge of material from the other two sections.

* <s>The aside {{tq|(cordelette)}} needs to be explained with its climbing context and properly integrated in the text; an illustration would make sense here to show what the term means and how the knot functions in this situation.</s>
:: I've added a picture and more of an explanation of what cordalettes are used for with a wikilink.

* <s>The use of three similar and somewhat repetitive infoboxes is undesirable; the information so presented would be better in a comparative table to avoid repetition, not to mention the lengthy use of screen real-estate down the side of a large part of the text. Really there should be at most 1 infobox, specially as it's agreed they are all closely related (or the merge would have been a mistake).</s>
::Yeah, when I did the merge and expanded the article I struggled with this. I've made it one infobox and I'll consider adding a comparison table to the end of the article (maybe with a gallery of other pictures from commons as well).
::: Sounds promising! 

* <s>'grapevine knot' is uncited; 'new' claims should not in any case be introduced in the lead section. 
The other alternative names are cited but the ref and the claims should be moved from lead to the article body.</s>
::That name is also in Ashley's book of Knots, I'll clarify and move everything to the history section.
:::Should be done now.

* <s>'reliability' is mentioned only in the lead; the claim should be introduced in the article body and the citation moved out of the lead.</s>
::I've rephrased it to just strength and added a line on it in the body with a note discussing what the sources mean by "strength".

* <s>'search and rescue' is mentioned only in the lead; the claim should be introduced in the article body and properly explained (are there considerations there different from climbing, for example? are there S&R applications where untying is not necessary? - seems surprising) and the citation moved out of the lead.</s>
:: I've added a sentence and a source to the uses section.

* <s>{{tq|The technique used in tying the knot is important to determining the behavior of the knot under load.}} This 'Security' claim is not explained so it comes across as mysterious; the only clue (on re-reading) is the oblique mention {{tq|the initial geometry}}: but two obscure claims don't add up to clarity.</s>
::I've reworked the paragraph, is it clearer now?
::: Much improved. 

* <s>'Uses' should have a paragraph on surgical usage, as currently the only mention is from Classical times.</s>
::Done, added three new sources.</s>
::: Feels much more complete now.

* <s>'[[Manila rope]]' should be wikilinked (with uppercase M).</s>
::Done

* <s>Insufficient use has been made of [1] Tong 2024, in particular of how the geometry of the knot changes during tightening with the two strangle knots moving together and apart.</s>
:: Added additional paragraph on the various behaviors of the knot under load.
::: Super.

* <s>[7] describes another use, 'handfasting' during a wedding. Should be in 'Uses'.</s>
::Done, with another note on it from abok.

== Images ==

* All three images are on Commons, are relevant, and suitably licensed.
::The images I've added are also all on commons

=== Comments === * The text contains a lot of TLAs (three-letter acronyms), ranging from some like [[RNA]] that may be familiar to many readers (still worth spelling it out, ribonucleic acid), to quite a few that will certainly be new to nearly all visitors to the page (DAg, RNP, and the more complex S-DAg, L-DAg, not to mention HDAg, HBsAg which are a struggle even for this biologist). It would be better to spell these out and to introduce them gently. * Here's an example: {{tq|Ribozyvirians have negative-sense single-stranded RNA (–ssRNA) genomes that are about 1.5–1.7 kilobases in length. The genome is a non-segmented, covalently-closed circular RNA (cccRNA) molecule that organizes into a rod-like shape due to a high amount of self-complementarity.}} The [https://hemingwayapp.com/readability-checker Hemingway readability checker] says the first sentence is "hard to read" and the second "very hard to read". It rates the sample Grade 15 ("Poor. Aim for 9.") and states that the average adult's reading level is 8 or 9. To reword this material, consider some of the terms that readers will not know: '''negative-sense'''; '''single-stranded RNA'''; genome (perhaps); '''kilobase'''; '''covalently-closed'''; '''cccRNA'''; '''self-complementarity'''. The same goes for much of the rest of the text. * The article would be much easier for Joe Public* to read with a new 'Context' section (just after the lead). The context should explain that life is cellular, but that viruses, while behaving like parasites, are not cells and are doubtfully even living. You can explain briefly that a virus is a bit of DNA or RNA packaged in an envelope; and that the envelope contains proteins which enable the virus to stick on to a cell and allow its DNA or RNA to enter the cell and start to replicate itself. I think you also need to have a small paragraph in 'Context' explaining what a [[ribozyme]] is, that they are capable of catalysing chemical reactions, including splicing bits of RNA itself. You can see that there is a lot here that readers need to know to read the rest of the article, so try to make it simple, clear, and richly wikilinked. And reliably-sourced. ::::: * Joe Public can read the ''Baseball Gazette'' and has heard of viruses which give you 'flu
and get into your computer. He may have heard of DNA somewhere. :* I've tried to make sure acronyms are introduced in an appropriate manner and tried to make the text less technical either through explanation or using wikilinks, including adding a sentence explaining what ribozymes are. Joshua, you may well be correct about scope, but as your question implies, different interpretations are possible, and we do not seem to be converging on a solution that way, not least because the section is already long and difficult. Could I therefore propose that we take a step back and consider how best to proceed.

==== 3 possible approaches ====
Firstly, I hope we can agree that the coverage of '8. Samādhi' is already considerably longer than that of the Ashtanga limbs 1. to 7.: it is around 880 words long, whereas for example '7. Dhyāna' is 250 words, '3. Āsana' is 240 words, and '6. Dhāraṇā' is only 90 words. 

Given the agreed [[WP:UNDUE]] tag on the section, this all means that the section '8. Samādhi' is around three times the desired length. 

The section is not only long but complex, technical, and hard to read. For instance the sentence {{tq|Vitarka (or avitarka) "deliberative," "with thought": According to the later commentarial tradition, citta is concentrated upon a gross object of meditation, an object with a manifest appearance that is perceptible to our senses.}} is 33 words. The [https://hemingwayapp.com/readability-checker Hemingway readability checker] scores it as "Post-graduate. Poor... very hard to read", with the advice "Aim for [school grade] 9". This means that it is unsuitable for Wikipedia's general readership.

There are three possible approaches to resolve this situation.

: A. Cut down the text to a simple summary of 250 words. 

: B. Move the text to a new subsidiary article '[[Samadhi in the Yoga Sutras]]'; write a simple 250-word summary of its text in its lead section; replace the current text of '8. Samādhi' with the wording of that lead section, supported by citations from the text.

: C. Merge the text to the existing article of wider scope, '[[Samadhi]]'. Draft a simple 250-word summary of the part of it which applies specifically to Patanjali's view of the topic, and replace the existing text of '8. Samādhi' with that summary.

I've marked the link to the '[[Samadhi]]' article as "broader" not just "further"; the '[[Samadhi in the Yoga Sutras]]' would be the "further" link. I hope this is all clear, and that we can agree on one of the three approaches. [[User:Chiswick Chap|Chiswick Chap]] ([[User talk:Chiswick Chap|talk]]) 09:04, 13 November 2026 (UTC)

== Adding to the [[Ecdysis]] article ==

Hi, and welcome to Wikipedia. It seems you want to write about [[Ecdysis]]. That article sketches out the basis of a large topic, but is currently very poorly [[WP:CITE|cited]]. Wikipedia works entirely from [[WP:RS|reliable sources]], which have to be cited in the article, immediately after the text that they support. Basically, every claim has to be derived from, and cited to, such a source, to permit other editors to [[WP:V|verify]] that the claim is correct. Editing Wikipedia therefore consists of finding suitable sources (textbooks, scientific papers, occasionally newspaper reports or websites of scientific institutions), studying them, paraphrasing them to create accurate readable text, and immediately citing the source used. This is roughly halfway between ordinary writing and writing a scientific paper or textbook. Good luck! == Tolkien, sources, and a tree of articles ==

Hi, I noticed the kerfuffle that followed your addition of some material on Finnish influences on Tolkien to the top-level [[J. R. R. Tolkien]] article. Your edit comment "added information without a source" was certainly true, which poses the question "Why?". 

Firstly, you must be aware that Wikipedia requires claims to be cited to [[WP:RS|reliable sources]]. You must surely also have noticed that the Tolkien article is highly conspicuous, and has indeed been formally reviewed, so every claim there, other than yours, was already suitably sourced. So, you can't really be surprised that an editor has already removed your unsourced material: anyone is free to do that at any time, without notice.

Secondly, if you follow a few of the many wikilinks in the Tolkien article, you will quickly discover that there are '''hundreds''' of articles in WikiProject Middle-earth, with that article at the top. Thus, there is a whole article called [[Influences on Tolkien]], which in turn links to articles on Beowulf's influence, and influences from Finnish, the classical world, Celtic, Shakespeare, and so on and so forth :

* [[J. R. R. Tolkien]]
** [[Influences on Tolkien]]
*** [[Beowulf and Middle-earth]]
*** ...
** [[Themes of The Lord of the Rings|Themes of ''The Lord of the Rings'']]
*** [[Sound and language in Middle-earth]]
*** ...

This means that the tree of articles contains '''much''' more material than could possibly be included at the top level. Your uncited addition was too detailed for the top level, or to put it another way inappropriately positioned in there, as well as uncited. It is in fact already covered in full, with a quotation and a source, in the appropriate place in the tree. 

Hope this is all clear to you. All the best, [[User:Chiswick Chap|Chiswick Chap]] ([[User talk:Chiswick Chap|talk]]) 07:03, 8 July 2026 (UTC)
